The first chapter:
[Salutation to] Him whose abode plays upon the lofty peaks of the mountain of refined gold,
who bears the form of Dharma, and whose glorious emblem is the great bull.
Having approached Anantarudra, who blazes with the proximity of the assembly of Pramathas, Dhiṣaṇa, exalted by his intellect, [attained his goal].
Repeatedly touching the pedestal of his glorious lotus feet with his head,
he joined his palms in reverence, propitiated him thoroughly, and spoke these words in a low voice.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, refuge of all knowledge!
If the compendia of the scriptures were not clearly revealed by you,"
Indeed, the world, devoid of knowledge, would sink into blinding darkness. || 4 ||
In this world, there is no beast more foolish than he who, without understanding the teachings contained in the scriptures concerning existence, considers himself to be wise. (5)
By the attainment of your grace, having drunk the nectar of your sacred teachings,
I have become like the preceptor of the gods, one who has accomplished his goal.
I have heard many auspicious portions derived from the Candrajñāna;
therefore, please out of compassion explain here the teaching of Śiva.
I have heard that the *mokṣadharma* is taught there in particular; by learning it, may I become one who has understood all that is to be known. (8)
Anantarudra said:
"O Preceptor of the Lord of the Three Heavens, you have indeed asked a fitting question with your wise intellect;
listen attentively, for I shall declare the teaching of Śiva."
The Definition of the Meaning of the Term Paśupati:
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, all who are subject to the cycle of transmigration are proclaimed as the *paśus* (bound souls) of the trident-bearing God of gods. (10)

Because he is the lord of those [individual souls], Śiva is remembered as Viśveśa and Paśupati; as their Lord (pati), he binds the individual souls (paśu) with the fetters (pāśa) of impurity (mala), māyā, and so forth.
3) That very [Lord], when properly worshipped with devotion, is the liberator of those [souls].
The twenty-four principles constitute the state of bondage (pāśatva).
These twenty-four principles consist of Māyā, Karma, and the Guṇas.
Objects of the senses are called "nooses," for they bind the individual soul.
Having bound the fettered beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass with these nooses, the Lord Maheśvara, the Sovereign God, causes them to perform their respective tasks.
By the command of Paraśiva, the principle of omniscience arises; by his command, the Prakṛti of Maheśa produces the intellect (buddhi) appropriate for Puruṣa.
That intellect produces the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the ego-sense [produces the elements]. || 14 ||
The eleven sense organs and likewise the five subtle elements [arose] from the command of Śiva, the god of gods, the bestower of auspiciousness. (15)
By his own most exalted command, even the subtle elements (tanmātra) successively bring forth all the great elements (mahābhūta) without exception. || 16 ||
By the command of Śiva, all the great elements (mahābhūtas) bring about the union with a body for all embodied beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. (17)
The functions of the intellect and the other faculties are as follows:
the intellect indeed determines; the ego-sense conceives of itself;
the mind also perceives, and the mental organ also forms volitions. (18)

And by means of his divine power of knowledge, the Lord perceives the objects of the senses—sound and the rest—individually through the ears and other organs; he perceives only what belongs to himself, and certainly nothing else.
Furthermore, those organs of action, such as speech and the rest, which were previously assigned,
perform their respective functions according to the command of Śiva, and nothing else.
Even sounds and the like are perceived, and words and the like are uttered;
for the most weighty command of Śambhu is indeed inviolable by all.
The description of the arising of the five elements provides space for all beings without exception;
space is omnipresent solely by the command of the Supreme Lord. (22)
By the command of Śarva, the Wind sustains the entire universe— both internal and external— through various names such as Prāṇa and others. (23)

By the command of the Supreme Lord, Agni carries the oblation to the gods and the ancestral offering to those who consume the offerings of the ancestors; he also performs the cooking and other such tasks. 24.
By the command of Śiva, the waters perform for all [the function] beginning with restoration to life;
by the command of the Lord of the Universe, the Earth constantly supports the world. (25)
By the command of Śiva alone do the guardians of the quarters proceed;
they protect the gods, slay the asuras, and guard the three worlds.
By his command—which cannot be transgressed by any of the gods—the Lord of the Devas [Indra] acts. (26)
By the command of Śiva, the Lord of Dharma inflicts suffering upon the living through diseases and torments upon the dead who have acted unrighteously. (27)
Nirṛti seizes away the fruits of the actions of those who have neglected their prescribed duties;
and by the command of Śaṅkara, she exercises sovereignty over the night-stalkers. 28.
Varuṇa also constantly exercises sovereignty over the waters, and by the command of the Supreme Lord, he binds those who deserve to be bound with his nooses. (29)
The Lord of Yakṣas, the master of wealth, constantly bestows riches upon all beings in accordance with their merit, by virtue of the command of the City-Destroyer (Śiva).
By the command of Śiva, the Lord perpetually brings about prosperity, wisdom for the highly intelligent, and the restraint of the wicked.
But Śeṣa, by the command of Śiva, supports the earth upon his head.
(p. 7) Precisely because of the teaching of Śiva, Brahmā and the others possess the agency of creation and so forth:
"By the command of the Lord, the four-faced one creates everything without exception."
Through his own three forms, he protects and, at the end, destroys.
Viṣṇu protects the universe by the command of the Lord of the Universe,
and likewise creates and devours it through his own forms.
At the end, Hara withdraws the entire universe by his very command;
yet the Soul of the Universe, divided threefold, also creates and protects it.
It is solely by the command of Śiva that Time and the other factors proceed;
Time creates everything, Time destroys all beings, and Time protects the universe, by the decree of the One who is the Death of Time. (35)
Sustaining the world with three parts and ordaining rain with his splendors, this Sun-god pours down rain in the sky by the command of the God of gods. (36)
(8) The moon causes the various herbs to flourish and gladdens all living beings; yet, by the command of the Moon-Adorned One (Śiva), it is also drunk by the gods. || 37 ||
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
the sky-dwellers, the Ṛṣis, the Siddhas, the Bhogins, human beings, and wild animals. || 38 ||
From the very teaching of Śiva comes the creation of all things, both moving and stationary:
beasts, birds, insects and the like, as well as immobile beings; rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes. (39)
The Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the scriptures, the mantras, the Soma sacrifices and so forth;
the worlds beginning from Kālāgni and ending with Śiva, together with their presiding deities.
Even the countless cosmic eggs and their surrounding envelopes [are contained within it].
Present, past, and future in their entirety; the cardinal directions and intermediate points; and the divisions of time, such as the *kalās* and so forth—[all these are within it]. (41)
p. 9) Everything whatsoever that is seen or even heard in this world proceeds solely from the teaching of Śiva.
All that was sustained by the power of Śaṅkara’s command. || 42 ||
By the power of his command, the earth, the mountains, the clouds, and the oceans remain here;
so too do the hosts of luminaries and the gods headed by Śakra—whatever exists, whether moving or stationary, conscious or unconscious.
Bondage and liberation belong to these beings—both bipeds and quadrupeds;
Lord Śiva is their master, and bondage and liberation certainly abide under his control. (44)
Through initiation, one attains the grace of Śiva;
therefore, one who desires liberation should practice the initiation of Śambhu, which severs the accumulation of bonds that cause endless birth and death. (45)
Without his grace, the liberation of living beings from bondage is not attained;
nor is his grace obtained without this initiation.
This is the instruction of the Vedas; indeed, this is the teaching of Śiva.
10) Regarding the Śāmbhava vow’s capacity to ward off worldly existence: it is adorned by the triad of initiations known as Vedha, Mantra, and Kriyā.
It is endowed with the purification of the six paths and is sustained by the compassion of the Guru.
The supreme practice consists of wearing sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, and the venerable liṅga. || 47 ||
This is indeed the Śāmbhava vow, uniquely enjoined by the Vedas and the Śāstras;
it is the sole cause for the grace of Śiva and the means for warding off worldly existence. 48.
Even each single limb of this [image] is proclaimed in the Śruti to grant liberation;
what then need be said regarding that which possesses all its limbs as bestowing emancipation? (49)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Preeminence of Śiva," in the section on Ritual (Kriyāpāda) within the Teaching of Śiva, in the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati, in the latter portion of the illustrious *Candrajñānāgama*. || 1 ||
The second chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O ocean of the nectar of all knowledge, whose sole ornament is compassion!
Understand the greatness of the ancillary rites of the Śāmbhavī vow.
Anantarudra said:
The eight enclosures are the Guru, the Linga, the mobile deity (jaṅgama), the sacred ford (tīrtha), and the bestower of grace (prasādaka).
The sacred ash, the rudrākṣa beads, and the mantras—these are known as the eight enclosures (āvaraṇas).
These, which are always dedicated solely to the task of warding off the multitude of worldly defects for the devotees of Śiva, are renowned by the name of the "coverings" (āvaraṇas).
1. The Nature and Greatness of the Eight: "I shall explain, in brief, the nature and the greatness of these eight starting from the beginning; listen with a one-pointed mind. (4)
(12) For the attainment of initiation for liberation, the Guru is the fundamental cause;
without the Guru, the means of practice are not sufficient for success.
But because he is to be instructed, the disciple is the cause of the teacher's respect;
therefore, one should practice respect toward the teacher with every effort.
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
Or rather, the Guru is indeed Śiva himself, abiding in the form of knowledge (vidyā).
The equality of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Guru in bestowing fruit: as is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru.
And the fruit resulting from the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Guru is identical.
This Guru is the essence of all gods and consists of all mantras;
therefore, with every effort, one should carry his command upon one's head.
The attainment of excellent fruit through the observance of the guru’s command:
"One who seeks the highest good should not transgress the guru’s command even in thought;
for by observing the guru’s command, one attains the perfection of knowledge. (10)
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, whatever action one may perform,
if one should do it in the presence [of the teacher], all that must be done with the teacher’s permission. (11)
One should not sit at will in the presence of the guru or in his house;
for the guru is the manifest God himself, and his home is a temple of the Divine.
Just as one would partake in the fruit of the sins of evildoers through association with them, so too does one partake in the fruit of their virtues through association with a teacher. || 13 ||
Just as gold here sheds its impurity through contact with fire,
even so does a human being shed their sin through contact with a guru.
Just as a blazing fire brings a piece of wood to its ultimate end by consuming it, so too does this satisfied Guru burn away one's sin in an instant. 15.
Through the anger of the guru comes total ruin;
one should not provoke the anger of the guru by thought, deed, or word.
For by his anger, one's lifespan, prosperity, knowledge, and virtuous actions are consumed. 16.
The sacrifices of those who act with anger toward him are fruitless;
the same applies to their restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas)—there is no need for further deliberation on this point. || 17 ||
A person should never speak words that are contrary to the guru;
if he should speak them, he will certainly fall into the most terrible Raurava hell. (18)
If its lack of qualities is proclaimed, one shall partake of a hundredfold lack of merit;
but if its qualities are proclaimed, likewise all the fruit of merit shall accrue. || 19 ||
A man should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to his guru, whether commanded or not;
he should perform his duty for him both in his presence and in his absence.
The conduct of a disciple upon the arrival of the teacher:
seeing the teacher approaching his own home, a person endowed with devotion should bow, offer him a seat, and sit down only with his permission. (21)
Whoever always drinks or holds with devotion the water that has washed the pair of feet of one’s own teacher is liberated from all sins.
Having placed sandalwood, unbroken rice, flowers, gold, betel-leaf,
and clothing into a vessel, the disciple should give them to the Guru, not by hand.
Having fed his own guru, the wise man should eat afterwards;
he who eats in front of the guru is called a betrayer of the guru. (24)
Then one should cause excellent betel-leaf to be offered to him with a vessel;
afterwards, having presented the desired articles and bowed down, one should ask for his forgiveness. || 25 ||
In all auspicious rites, such as marriages and the like,
a disciple should worship the guru with devotion by offering garments and golden rings.
If he is poor, the disciple, without deceiving his own capacity regarding these prescribed [offerings], must certainly worship the Guru with whatever wealth he has obtained.
The Superiority of the Fruit of the Guru’s Pilgrimage:

The pilgrimage to the guru is threefold—namely, the pilgrimage to the deity, the pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrtha), and the pilgrimage to the guru. Among these three types of pilgrimages, the pilgrimage to the guru yields the greatest fruit. (28)
He who undertakes a journey with devotion for the purpose of beholding the Guru should be known as a meritorious being, beloved by all the immortals. (29)
A disciple entering a village where his teacher resides should avoid riding on vehicles and the like; likewise, he should avoid sandals in the vicinity of the teacher's house.
(p. 16) The Procedure for Serving the Guru:
A disciple who desires to see the Guru should, with true devotion and joy, [attend upon him] every day.
Just as one with empty hands should not appear before a king, so too should one not appear before a teacher.
Having offered one of these— fruit, a flower, betel, or some other object— to the teacher, he should then pay homage to the teacher.

Even one who is illustrious, ascetic, learned in the scriptures, and possessed of noble birth and character, should perform a prostration with his staff-like body in the presence of the Guru, for he is free from shame before him. (33)
Among all forms of service, only two are considered exceedingly beautiful: pleasant speech and prostration; without these, all others are deemed in vain. (34)
Having seen the Guru in front, having paid homage, and recollecting the circumambulation,
one should perform the circumambulation according to one's capacity. || 35 ||
The wise person who knows how to circumambulate should not place his feet too far apart;
the wise person should not walk hurriedly, nor should he speak with others.
Placing one foot after the other, with hands free from movement, one should perform circumambulation while offering praise with speech and meditation with the heart. (37)
17) Regarding the conduct of a disciple before his guru:
in the presence of his own guru, the disciple should not mention other people.
And one should not speak to one another with words that are unbearable to hear.
One should never speak a falsehood, nor an unpleasant word, nor even a secret;
one should never speak with an uncovered mouth in the presence of the guru. (39)
The Guru should always be addressed by his disciples using the titles "Svāmin," "Bhaṭṭāraka," "Ācārya," "Deva," or "Śrī-guru," and never by any other names. (40)
A disciple should never address his teacher by the word "thou" (tvaṃ);
he should not disobey his command, nor should he sit on an equal level with him. || 41 ||
Those who desire progress, perfection, and welfare should not make their seat, vehicle, clothing, ornaments, or bed resemble those of the Guru. (42)
One should not touch with one's feet, nor step over, the alms-bowl, the water for bathing, the shade [of the deity], garlands, or ritual implements—even if one is devoid of devotion. (43)
Neglecting the guru is destructive for that disciple who views the guru like an ordinary person;
O wise one, his devotion is in vain—of this there is no doubt. (44)
The sinful soul who neglects the Guru— the abode of all deities and the locus of all mantras— shall go to the Raurava hell. (45)
The Greatness of Devotion to the Guru:
O Wise One, for a disciple who possesses absolute devotion toward the guru, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain in this world or the next; rather, everything is always easily obtained. (46)
Thus, a disciple who possesses proper conduct, who is constantly diligent in mind through devotion, and who acts to please the guru, is worthy of all dharmas. (47)
The characteristics of the Guru:
The Guru is virtuous, wise, and the illuminator of supreme bliss;
he is a knower of reality, devoted to Śiva, and the bestower of liberation—none other than him.
One who knows the reality of the Śaiva Siddhānta, who has mastered the mantras for consecration, who bestows liberation, who is endowed with compassion, free from passion, and devoid of envy. (49)

The definitive realization of the Śiva-principle, beginning with ritual action and culminating in knowledge, [is attained] by one who possesses knowledge received through the tradition and has arisen from a lineage of gurus. (50)
One who knows the distinctions between the *liṅga*, the limbs, and the locations; one who is devoted to the knowledge of the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*);
one skilled in the rites of initiation and so forth; and one who is fond of the knowledge of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*). || 51 ||
He was a devotee of Śiva and his guru, with his mind solely intent on Śiva;
his heart was absorbed in the worship of Śiva, and he was single-mindedly devoted to meditation upon Śiva. || 52 ||
The justification for the status of the householder as the preceptor:
Only the householder may be the preceptor; a renunciant (yati) can never be a preceptor. For forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) and renunciants, the status of being a preceptor would be fruitless. (53)
The Determination of the True Nature of the Guru: There are many gurus who plunder the wealth of their disciples;
rare in this world is that guru who removes the darkness from the heart of the disciple. (54)
That reality which generates consciousness, which is true, and from which supreme bliss arises—only he by whom that reality is known is the one who reveals bliss. (55)
Furthermore, that which is devoid of realization exists as a mere name;
such an ignorant person cannot deliver another—can a stone deliver a stone? || 56 ||
(20) This liberation is indeed merely nominal, existing only by name.
But those by whom reality has been realized are truly liberated and they liberate others as well. 57.
How can there be awakening in one devoid of reality? How indeed can there be the grasping of a self?
One who is liberated from grasping is called a "beast" (paśu). || 58 ||
Even if impelled by other beings, one does not transcend the state of being a beast;
therefore, having realized the truth in this world, one is considered liberated and a liberator.
Even if one is endowed with all auspicious marks, even if one knows all the scriptures,
and even if one is an expert in all methods and procedures, if one is devoid of the ultimate reality (tattva), it is fruitless.
The characteristics of a wicked preceptor are as follows:
one who is addicted to vice, a dwarf, a hunchback, one prone to anger, crooked, a rogue, fickle, one with extra or missing limbs, a sinner, a slanderer, or an outcaste. (61)

One afflicted by disease, a sophist, a hero, one who caws like a crow, one who observes the vow of a heron, a reviler of gurus, gods, and the twice-born, and the husband of a low-caste woman; || 62 ||
One who has drooping lips, a crooked nose, and a slumped neck; one who is fond of quarreling and habitually speaks ill of others—such a teacher is said to be avoided. (63)
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own self-interest, crafty, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata).
For one whose mind, having reached the culmination of realization, is firmly established in reality through the selection of a worthy guru,
supreme bliss arises by means of his glance and other such acts. (65)
Therefore, a wise man should choose only that very teacher through whose contact the arising of awakening-bliss occurs, and no other.
Regarding the characteristics of a disciple and his duties:
first, having approached a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas, he should propitiate a wise, fortunate, and pleasant-looking guru. (67)
One should strive to please with mind, deed, and speech that giver of all that can be told, whose mind is overcome by compassion. 68.
The disciple should propitiate [the teacher] until he becomes pleased;
when he is pleased, the destruction of the disciple’s bonds occurs instantly. (69)
Therefore, [give] wealth, jewels, fields, and houses; ornaments, garments, vehicles, beds, and seats. (70)
One should give these to the guru with devotion according to one's means;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires the supreme goal. (71)
He alone is one's father, mother, brother, kinsman, and friend; he is one's very self and one's wealth.
Therefore, one should offer everything to him. 72.
Having first offered himself, along with his lineage and his dependents,
and having respectfully surrendered them to Him, he should remain perpetually subject to His will.
When one has offered one’s own self to Śiva, who is the soul of the Guru, then that embodied being becomes a devotee of Śiva (Śaiva); from that point on, there is no further rebirth.
Assuming the form of a guide, the Lord undoubtedly leads this bound soul to the supreme state after severing all its fetters without exception.
Regarding the examination of the disciple: the guru, however, should examine the disciple who has taken refuge in him for one year;
or, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, for two or three years respectively. (76)
By means of bestowing life-force, wealth, and other such gifts, as well as through various commands— both equal and unequal—
they cause the superior to become inferior and the lowly to perform the highest deeds. (77)
Those who do not fall into despondency even when dragged or beaten are always fit and pure for the rite of Śiva’s consecration.
They were non-violent, compassionate, always possessed of a diligent mind, free from pride, wise, devoid of rivalry, and sweet-spoken. (79)
The twice-born were upright, gentle, pure, humble, and firm-minded; they were endowed with purity and right conduct and were devotees of Śiva. 80.

Thus, those endowed with proper conduct through the actions of speech, mind, and body should be purified and awakened according to what is right; such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures. (81)
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when one's own true Guru is angry, Śiva is the protector. Therefore, for this reason, one should be devoted to the worship of the Guru.
He who abandons the worship of his own guru and worships the state of Śiva instead—Śiva turns his face away from him and consigns him to hell. || 83 ||
Having fully understood all these fruits of honoring the guru, one should personally perform worship of the guru.
The Guru, fully satisfied by the worship, bestows his own state of union.
On Mondays during the month of Kārttika, one should worship with flowers, leaves, and fruits;
if capable, one should do so for the entire month without weariness.
Or one should worship at the three times of day, or at the six times, or at twilight.
Adorned with ornaments of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, muttering the five-syllable mantra,
Bhūti quickly approached his guru and [prostrated at] his lotus feet.
Having paid homage with devotion, he should lead that guru back toward his own home.
When the Guru has arrived at one's home, one should honor him by placing him upon a palanquin, or even upon an elephant or a horse;
then, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments, one should follow him personally with devotion.
Having led the preceptor into the house, he then washed his two feet;
with that water, he sprinkled his head along with his own kinsmen.
Having given him a hand to hold and led him into the interior of the house,
he prepared an excellent seat and seated him with affection.
One should worship the imperishable Guru according to the prescribed injunctions. || 89 ||
During the time of the worship of the Guru, a wise person should daily light one hundred and eight lamps, or thirty-six, according to his capacity.
On the thirteenth day and subsequent days, one should worship the Guru in the auspicious pavilion.

Whatever was previously spoken by the Guru—whether it be possible or indeed impossible—that one whose soul is purified certainly performs, even at the cost of life and wealth; that disciple should offer everything, including his body and all else, to the Guru. (91)
One of firm vows should worship the devotees of Maheśvara, together with their wives, along with their own wife, using food and other offerings— whether five, ten, or a hundred of them.
Having first offered the finest portion, one should eat with the permission of the guru. || 92 ||
One should worship with wealth in the form of sandals and the like, by massaging the feet and so forth, and also with bathing, anointing, food offerings, and meals.
Receiving [the teachings] through the grace of the Guru is itself the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
indeed, everything remaining from the Guru becomes the means for purifying one's own self. (94)
Therefore, having learned the ritual action and especially the knowledge from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform everything in its entirety for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation. (95)
He who is a vessel for the grace of the Guru is indeed fit for liberation;
for there is no other root of liberation than the excellent compassion of the Guru. (96)

The form of the Guru, the Teacher of the Gods, [is manifested] out of a desire to bestow grace upon the worlds; this is declared to be the first enclosure (āvaraṇa). What do you wish to hear after this? (97)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Guru," in the section on Ritual Practice (*kriyāpāda*) of the *Śivaśāsana*, within the dialogue between Ananta Rudra and Bṛhaspati in the *Śrīcandrajñānāgama*.
The third chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O abode of infinite knowledge, you who are intent upon the grace of the worlds!
O Lord Anantarudra, I am blessed by your grace. || 1 ||
Having heard again and again from the glorious mouth of my most excellent Guru the boundless extent of [the teachings], I am submerged in an ocean of intense bliss. (2)
Now, O Compassionate One, please tell me about the second most purifying Śiva-liṅga, which I am eager to hear about— its form and its greatness.
Anantarudra said:
"O Bṛhaspati, behold! I shall explain the nature of the Great Liṅga, knowing which a living being is liberated without delay."
2. Regarding the nature and majesty of the Liṅga:
formerly, when the world had perished in a terrible single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had vanished, the supreme, fiery Liṅga of Īśvara arose in the midst [of the waters].
Enveloped in garlands of flames, divine, immeasurable, and free from ailment—
therein all the deities dissolve at the end of the eon and abide.
And in the heart is the Gāyatrī, the most excellent among all the gods;
indeed, the Vedas, together with their six ancillaries and the methods of Pada and Krama, dissolve into the crown of the head. (7)
The entire world, both stationary and moving, dissolves into its belly;
since it is from that [source] that it arises again, that Brahman is designated by the term "liṅga. (8)
The unmanifest is declared to be the subtle mark (liṅga), infinite, undecaying, and eternal;
it is that very Lord who creates, protects, and destroys the three qualities (guṇas).
The Śiva-liṅga is fourfold;
indeed, that very Śiva-liṅga is of four types:
the Supreme Bindu, the Supreme Nāda, and the two others, Bindu and Nāda.
O you who are worshipped by the gods, these four also have their lower and upper portions as their limits.
Below is the lower *bindu*, above that is another *dhvani*;
above that would be the supreme *bindu*, and the supreme *nāda* moves above that.
The *praṇava* is its altar, and this resonance (*nāda*) in the form of a *liṅga* is at its mouth; Śiva is eternally present in the *liṅga* composed of *bindu* and *nāda*. (12)
The universe consists of *bindu* and *nāda*; the entire universe, both mobile and immobile, consists of *bindu* and *nāda*.
*Bindu* is Śakti and *nāda* is Śiva; the universe is composed of Śiva and Śakti. (13)
The Bindu has Nāda as its support, and this world has the Bindu as its support;
for indeed, the Bindu and Nāda are established as the foundational supports of the world. (14)
Everything joined with Bindu and Nāda becomes the process of Sakalīkaraṇa;
through Sakalīkaraṇa, the world undoubtedly attains birth. || 15 ||
The Liṅga, which consists of Bindu and Nāda, is said to be the cause of the universe;
therefore, for the sake of ending rebirth, one should worship the Śiva-liṅga. || 16 ||
The Mother Goddess is in the form of the Bindu (the Point), and Śiva, the Father, is in the form of Nāda (the Sound).
Just as the sovereignty bestowed by the parents is made available for enjoyment, so too should one worship the Śivaliṅga for the sake of attaining the sovereignty of those two. || 17 ||
The Śiva-liṅga has the form of the mother and father;
she is the Goddess, the mother of the worlds, and he is Śiva, the father of the worlds.
Indeed, for one who is constantly devoted to the service of his parents, compassion increases ever further.
Indeed, out of compassion, he bestows upon the worshiper the sovereignty contained within himself.
Therefore, O bull among sages, for the sake of attaining the bliss contained within, one should worship the Śivaliṅga, which is indeed the very form of one’s father and mother. (19)
The nature of the Great Liṅga is partless, actionless, tranquil, faultless, and stainless;
it is that in which all distinctions have subsided, which is pure existence alone, and beyond the reach of the senses.
That which is self-evident through words is called the Great Linga.
The Supreme Brahman is the eternal law (ṛta), the truth (satya), characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
that Brahman, who is none other than the Supreme, should therefore be meditated upon by the faithful. || 21 ||
Then, having renounced everything and being solely intent upon the Great Liṅga,
one should become free from possessiveness and egoism, devoted to meditation upon that.
(31) The threefold nature of the Great Liṅga:
The Great Liṅga has arisen in three ways out of a desire to favor virtuous people.
The first is the liṅga of existence (bhāvaliṅga), the second is the liṅga of vital breath (prāṇaliṅga), and the third is the chosen liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga); thus it is considered to be threefold.
The partless (niṣkala) symbol of existence (bhāvaliṅga) is perceivable through pure being and is higher than the highest;
the vital-force symbol (prāṇaliṅga), perceivable by the mind, is both with parts and partless (sakalaniṣkala).
The entire [liṅga] perceivable by the faculty of sight is proclaimed as the *iṣṭaliṅga*;
it perfectly accomplishes one's desired goals and wards off the undesired. (25)
The examination of the sixfold signs:
the triad of signs beginning with *bhāva* is each of two kinds.
The sign of *bhāva* consists of the two known as the *mahāliṅga* and *prasāda*. (26)
Likewise, there are the two moving Śiva-liṅgas known as Prāṇaliṅga;
furthermore, there are the two pairs known as the Guru-liṅga (the desired) and the Ācāra-liṅga (conduct). || 27 ||
The conduct-liṅga is declared to have the face of Sadyojāta as its essence;
likewise, the guru-liṅga should have the face of Vāmadeva as its essence. (28)
Likewise, the Śiva-liṅga may further take the form of the face of Aghora;
it indeed becomes a mobile liṅga (cara-liṅga) consisting of the face of Tatpuruṣa.
The Prasādaliṅga is said to be designated by the name Īśānamukha;
likewise, the Mahāliṅga is proclaimed to be the form of Akhaṇḍa Śiva. (30)
Śiva is to be worshipped in an installed linga; through the complete worship and meditation upon the linga, Śambhu becomes perfectly pleased.
Indeed, Śiva is present within the linga when it is meditated upon and worshipped.
Therefore, O learned one, the supreme Śiva should be worshipped daily in the chosen liṅga,
and the Lord of Ambikā, in the form of the liṅga, should be constantly meditated upon.
The meditation on the Prāṇaliṅga in the Ādhāra and other locations is proclaimed as follows:
the Prāṇaliṅga is described as resembling gold in the Ādhāra, possessing the luster of coral in the heart, and appearing like a lamp in the space between the eyebrows. (33)
O learned one, this Jyotirliṅga is the place of meditation for Maheśvara;
having clearly contemplated the Jyotirliṅga, the Supreme Śiva is to be meditated upon there. (34)
Within the vital breaths, the mind has its abode; that auspicious Linga situated in the heart-lotus is what should be grasped here, known by the name Prāṇaliṅga.
That very place, which is the form of light, is the primary abode of Maheśvara;
meditating upon Him there, Śambhu indeed liberates one without delay.
The definition of the existential sign (bhāvaliṅga) is that which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss; it is peaceful and devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
That which is partless and belonging to Śambhu, though formless, is called the Form.
O learned one, that which is the locus for its cultivation is proclaimed as the *bhāvaliṅga*. || 37 ||
That which is graspable through meditative cultivation, transcending the mind, beyond existence and non-existence, auspicious,
the truth that brings about the creation of the constituent parts (kalās), is proclaimed as the Bhāvaliṅga.
Yogis whose collection of senses has been withdrawn and who have found their footing in the state beyond the mind should cultivate that state known as the "Beyond-the-Fourth" (turīyātīta). || 39 ||
The great-souled yogis, who have forgotten all other states of being and have realized the indivisible reality, constantly meditate upon the Bhāvaliṅga.
Through the experience of the signs of their inner state, they are oceans of the nectar of supreme bliss;
free from desire, fearless, and peaceful, they are undoubtedly liberated while living. (41)
The worship of the three genders: the light-form *prāṇaliṅga* is established within the lotus of the heart.
Or, according to the faithful, it should be meditated upon in the heart, between the eyebrows, or in the fourth state (turiya). || 42 ||
The external location for the meditation and worship of Śambhu is desired;
it should be resorted to during the waking state by those who seek the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (43)
In the same way, the inner station is proclaimed as the *prāṇaliṅga*;
this should be cultivated by those seeking liberation from the bonds of worldly existence within the fourth state (*turīya*).

The "desired" (iṣṭa) is said to belong to the gross body, while the "vital breath" (prāṇa) is remembered as belonging to the subtle body; thus, the threefold [causes] residing in the three bodies are designated as the "state" (bhāva) of the cause. 45.
Initiation is that which destroys the three impurities—the Āṇava, the Māyika, and the Kārmika—in their respective order. This beginningless triad of impurities resides within the three bodies. (46)
Having burnt away these three impurities (*mala*) residing in the three bodies by means of the three initiations, the Guru should teach the three signs (*liṅga*).
The greatness of worshipping the three genders: "Worshipping the chosen *liṅga* while meditating upon the *prāṇa-liṅga*."
Indeed, by meditating upon the linga of existence, he cuts the nooses of death.
The Liṅga consists of all the gods; within it, Śiva himself dwells in person for the sake of bestowing grace. Therefore, one should worship the Liṅga. (49)
Whatever holy fords and sacred shrines exist upon the earth, they all dissolve into the base of the Liṅga; therefore, one should worship the Liṅga.
They say that space is the *liṅga* and the earth is its pedestal;
it is called the *liṅga* because it is the abode of all beings and because of its dissolution [into the source]. || 51 ||
But he who constantly worships the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds, quickly becomes a recipient of the entire kingdom of liberation. || 52 ||
All worlds consist of the Liṅga; everything is established in the Liṅga.
Therefore, one should worship the Liṅga if one desires one's own perfection.
O Preceptor of the Gods, I have explained the true nature of the Śivaliṅga and its eternal majesty; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Liṅga," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Compassionate One, O Omniscient One, you who are ever intent upon bestowing grace upon your devotees!
O Anantarudra, treasure-trove of the nectar of all scriptures, salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
I am blessed by having heard the majesty of the Śiva-liṅga;
please, out of your grace, tell me also the characteristics and the greatness of the mobile liṅga (jaṅgama).
Anantarudra said:
Oh, listen now as I explain the majesty of the mobile world, which is hidden within the conclusions of the scriptures; by knowing which, one attains immortality. (3)
3–4. The characteristic of the mobile and its majesty: it is remembered that Śambhu has two forms, the mobile and the immobile.
And the immobile is twofold: the self-manifested and the installed.
In that place, Viśveśvara and other deities may be self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta),
or they may be established by humans through rites such as plowing and consecration.
The mobile [deity] is of two kinds;
the mobile is said to be twofold: the mantra-born and the innate.
The mantra-born [deity] is invoked and manifested through the power of the mantra.
O Sage, the mobile liṅgas and other such objects are maintained by the great Śaivas.
The innate mobile [form] is designated as "Māheśvara";
the devotee who moves about is a Māheśvara, a Śaiva, and also a Jaṅgama.
The designations for the Sahaja arise from the teaching of the Lord. || 7 ||
The three types of Sahajajaṅgamas are the celibate student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhī), and the one who bears no burden (nirābhārī);
these three are distinguished in ascending order and are to be honored according to the prescribed rule.
I shall describe the marks of devotion; the marks of devotion are: affection for wearing rudrākṣas, faith in the triple-crested mark of ashes, and trust in the auspicious five-syllabled mantra.
Attachment to the purity of Śiva, great reverence for the wearing of the *liṅga*,
supreme delight in the other [the Guru], and mastery of the mind through service to Śiva. (10)
"Have supreme faith in the Śaiva scriptures, their daily teaching, and your own study as well; determine these to be the characteristics of one who possesses the moving Lakṣmī."
O Bṛhaspati, there are ten external marks for those who possess the ten marks of the mobile [devotees];
the first is said to be the wearing of ashes, rudrākṣas, and the liṅga.
The second is service to the guru, and the third is the hymn to Śiva.
The utterance of the Lord’s name is proclaimed as the fourth;
the fifth is declared to be the worship of the God of gods. (13)
The sixth is declared to be the investigation into the meaning of the Śiva-āgamas;
likewise, they know the seventh to be the hearing of the Śiva-purāṇas. (14)
The eighth is proclaimed as the salutation to those who move about (the wandering ascetics),
and the ninth is said to be the offering of food at the home of Śiva’s devotees.
Generosity is to be known as the tenth, even when the Guru is mobile;
thus, exactly ten external signs have been described.
p.
40) Three internal signs have been described for the great-souled ones; three internal signs have been declared.
Listen, O wise one, to those [methods], of which the first is mental recitation (mānasa-japa). || 17 ||
The mental worship of the Supreme Lord is to be known as the second;
the third, however, is the direct realization of the Supreme Lord within one's own self. (18)
Furthermore, when those who possess both internal and external [qualities] exist, they indeed come to have ten other signs. (19)
There are ten other signs: first, a change in the throat; second, what is called a faltering voice; third, trembling of the tongue; and also throbbing of the lips. (20)
Trembling of the body is the fourth characteristic of devotion;
horripilation is the fifth, and perspiration is proclaimed as the sixth. (21)
The seventh sign to be known is stumbling; the eighth is the shedding of tears;
the ninth sign is weeping; and the tenth is being under another's control.
These ten signs of devotion have been declared by the Wielder of the Trident.
Those great souls who possess these aforementioned marks should be known as devotees of Śaṅkara, the sole purifiers of all the worlds. (23)
The greatness of devotion is boundless; by whom can that greatness of devotion be described?
For even the God of gods considers his own devotees to be superior to himself.
Agastya, born from a jar, drank the incomparable ocean solely through devotion to Śiva, being empowered by that very devotion to Śiva.
The minute attains greatness, and the great may enter into minuteness;
dry land becomes the ocean, and the ocean may turn into dry land. (26)
How and by whom can the greatness of those who are endowed with the experience of Śiva—whose majesty is beyond the reach of speech and mind—be described, when it arises from mere volition? 27.
Therefore, devotees are the most excellent; this was declared by Śiva himself in the past:
"Whatever my devotees desire, even if it be difficult to obtain within the three worlds,"
I shall accomplish that immediately; this vow is always mine.
The greatness of the mobile [deity] consists of worldly and otherworldly enjoyments as well as liberation; through association with it, one becomes possessed of these.
Indeed, association with the mobile [deity] bestows the fruits of all desires upon everyone. || 29 ||
A dwelling purified by the dust of his feet is superior to any other forest;
therefore,
one who desires their own welfare should honor such a wandering ascetic to the best of one's ability.
Since these beings, though possessing human forms, have directly perceived the Supreme Lord. || 30 ||
Devotion toward a mobile [liṅga] is of three kinds.
Devotion toward one's own chosen mobile liṅga is called the highest; devotion toward a mobile liṅga that is equal [to one's own] is declared to be middling. (31)
When one's practice is inferior to that of one's chosen deity, it is called "inferior devotion" (kaniṣṭhā-bhakti).
Therefore, a skillful person should always resort to the highest form of devotion (uttamā-bhakti). || 32 ||
The worship of the *caru* is more weighty than bathing at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and than the performance of all sacrifices;
the worship of the *caru* is more weighty even than the propitiation of all the gods. (33)
Having seen him from afar, one should approach the Great Lord (Maheśa), salute him, and bring him home; "He is to be sacrificed to"—this is the command of Śiva.
"The world would be devoted to what is beneficial, while I would delight in what is not beneficial"—thinking thus, one should perform sacrifices well; such is the teaching of Śiva. (35)
"If my worship is performed without first worshipping the moving and the non-moving, that worship shall indeed be fruitless; such is the command of Śiva. (36)
Then, desiring what is beneficial for oneself, one should honor the attendants;
that which brings satisfaction to their minds is declared to be true worship. (37)
This, your final majesty, which grants the accomplishment of the goals of worldly enjoyment and liberation, has now been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (38)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Mobile [Embodiment]," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the Anantarudra-Bṛhaspati-saṃvāda of the Uttarabhāga of the Candrajñānāgama. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O abode of all knowledge, you who are intent upon the grace of the worlds!
O Rudra of infinite majesty, O ocean of boundless greatness, salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
O Soul of the Universe, having heard from Your glorious mouth of the infinite majesty of the moving Śiva-yogins here, I have attained my life’s purpose.
Today, desiring to serve the abundance of the grace of Your feet and the water used for washing them, I have made my request;
O Lord of the Universe, please favor me with Your compassion. (3)
Anantarudra said:
Listen, I shall describe to you the true nature and the majesty of Pādatīrtha and Prasāda, as revealed by the Lord.
The threefold nature of the sacred water of the feet: O, the sacred water of the feet of Śambhu, as well as that of the Guru and the Jaṅgama,
indeed possesses these three designations— initiation (dīkṣā), instruction (śikṣā), and knowledge (jñāna).
The established rule regarding the water from the feet of the Guru,

the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama is that those seeking liberation from the bonds of worldly existence should always drink this "foot-tīrtha," especially that of the Guru, the beloved Liṅga, and the mobile [Jaṅgama].

(45) In the absence of the Guru’s water from his feet, one should obtain the water from the feet of a chosen *liṅga* or a sacred footprint; having obtained that, one should contemplate it as being the very water from the feet of the Guru and others, by means of the mind alone.

Except for the alms-food, when receiving a gift from the Guru, one should reflect: "Having received the water from the feet of the Guru, I have now obtained the water from the feet of the Guru’s living representative. || 8 ||
When the turn comes for the other [disciples] except for the Guru, having received the water from the feet of the one currently serving,
one should drink it at that time, considering it to be the very water from the Guru’s feet.
Having offered water for the feet to that Lord, one should take the water from His feet with the "Hundred-stream" mantra joined with the five-syllabled mantra.
By placing the water from the feet upon one's head, one obtains great fruit;
and by drinking it while reciting "Ṛtaṃ Satyam," one enjoys infinite reward.
The auspicious water from the feet of Śambhu destroys untimely death, annihilates all diseases, and pacifies all sins. (12)
It is the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the purifier of all purifiers, the pacifier of malevolent planets, and the bestower of the fulfillment of desired goals. (13)
It pacifies all suffering, destroys all calamities,
bestows all accomplishments immediately, and grants liberation to everyone. (14)
The single form has three parts: the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama.
Therefore, that which possesses these qualities should be accepted in the case of both the Guru and the Jaṅgama as well. (15)
The greatness of the water from the feet of the Guru dries up the mire of sin and kindles the light of knowledge;
wonderful indeed is the water from the Guru’s feet, which destroys the tree of worldly existence.
Indeed, that purity which arises in the mind from bathing at all sacred fords is truly attained when the water from touching the feet of the Guru is borne upon one's head.
The fruit of bathing at all sacred fords throughout the seven oceans can never equal even a thousandth part of a single drop of water from the feet of the Guru.
Who is able to describe the greatness of the washing of his feet?
For that [water] is capable of immediately liberating all things, both moving and unmoving.
5. The Nature and Majesty of Prasāda:
Now I shall speak of the nature of *prasāda*; listen to its majesty.
The remains of what has been eaten by the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama is *prasāda*. || 20 ||
Faith is of three kinds, known as śuddha (pure), siddha (accomplished), and prasiddha (renowned); for it is the sole means to liberation.
Upon obtaining two or all three, this [śuddha] should be accepted, like a sacred ford at the foot of a tree.
One should eat what has been eaten by Śiva, drink the water he has drunk, and always smell what has been smelled by Śiva; this is the eternal dharma.
Only that grace which is offered to Śiva is to be accepted;
however, those deluded ones who eat what has not been offered to Tryambaka eat excrement and go forever to the lower realms. (23)
One should never consume a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, food, drink, or medicine without first offering them to the Blessed One, Sadāśiva. (24)
One should not enjoy [the objects of the senses] without first offering the five subtle elements— sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— to the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Umā.
Whatever pleasure has come through the senses, that is offered to Śiva;
it should be enjoyed as His grace, and by means of those very senses. 26.
In unions and in separations, as well as in pleasures even as small as an atom,
one should constantly enjoy them only after offering them to the desired deity.
Dedication is said to be twofold, distinguished as gross and subtle;
that which is dedicated to the chosen *liṅga* without any distinction from sound and the other [objects of the senses].
That substance is said to be gross; it is proclaimed as a limb of the image.
That in which objects such as sound and the rest are presented through their very essence and not otherwise—that indeed is proclaimed as the gross (or subtle) form. (29)
The gross aspect of the object of worship is said to be the "limb of the image" (arcāṅga), while the subtle aspect is that which pertains to experience;
this occurs at the time of experiencing objects such as sound and the rest, through their various distinctions.
For that dedication is subtle; this [present one] shall be perpetual. || 30 ||
When an object is experienced by means of a particular sense organ, its subtle offering into the sign (liṅga) residing in that very sense organ is declared [to be the practice]. (31)
Those devotees who correctly understand the excellence of this dedication indeed obtain the incomparable and effortless grace of Śambhu.
Its characteristic is serenity and its majesty is bestowed because it is the sole cause of the Great Lord’s grace;
renowned as serenity itself, it bestows supreme bliss. (33)
The Supreme Brahman is sung of as Ṛta, Satya, and Amṛta;
by whom or how can its grace and majesty be described? (34)
One should especially consume the remains of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) left by the Guru;
indeed, the grace of both the teacher and the ritual (cara) is certainly a bestower of purity.
O Preceptor of the Gods, the inconceivable greatness of your grace has been declared; it must be guarded with great effort. What else do you wish to hear? (36)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Grace of Water from the Feet," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 5 ||
The sixth chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Lord of the World, enriched with immeasurable power, salutations be unto you!
Having heard this ground of serene faith, I have now accomplished my purpose. || 1 ||
Out of compassion, please also reveal the unsurpassed majesty of the sixth ash, and thereby make me blessed this very day.
Anantarudra said:
"O Brahman, I shall explain the preparation of the ashes, as well as their wearing and their majesty; listen with an attentive mind. (3)
6. The sixth enclosure is called Bhasma.
Vidyā-śakti is designated as the power of all;
Vidyā rests upon the three qualities (guṇas), and that [power] rests upon Vidyā. (44)
The description of the true nature of the cow, the cow-dung, and the cow-urine:
This threefold quality is the Cow; the auspicious cow-dung is Knowledge (Vidyā); the urine is said to be the Upaniṣad. Thereafter, one should prepare the sacred ash (bhasma).
Regarding the procedure for preparing the ashes:
one should consecrate the cow there with the five-syllable mantra;
then, having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should cause her to consume water and grass.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight, the observer of the vow,
having risen early the following morning, shall become pure and composed in mind. (7)
Having bathed and put on clean clothes, he should release a cow for the sake of milk;
having raised the cow with effort, he should collect the urine while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should hold it in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay;
or in a vessel made of lotus leaves, or of Palāśa leaves, or even in a cow's horn.
One should indeed take cow’s urine with the root mantra and cow dung;
one should collect it in the previously mentioned vessel at home, without letting it fall upon the ground.
The wise one should purify the cow dung with eight recitations of the root mantra;
likewise, he should purify the cow urine with the mantra recited ten times.
One should pour cow's urine into the cow dung with the mantra "Bhavāya namaḥ," and likewise,
one should prepare fourteen balls [of clay] with the mantra "Śarvāya namaḥ."
Having dried it with rays [of light], one should extract it with the root-mantra of the Seven Mothers;
then, one should place balls of cow-dung into the previously mentioned vessel.
(p. 53) Having established the fire according to the procedure taught in the Śaiva Āgamas, one should worship it by performing the oblation ritual (āhuti-vidhāna).
And one should cast the morsels of food there with the Praṇava at the beginning and the end.
There, one should offer balls of cow dung with the syllables of the six-syllable mantra, which are thus reversed and end in *svāhā*.
Restrained, he should offer the two portions of clarified butter with the root mantra alone;
then he offers the twenty-third oblation to Nidhanapati.
Those known as the five Brahmans are to be offered; obeisance to the god Śambhu. || 16 ||
Having thus offered all the oblations with mantras ending in the dative case—
namely Bhava, Śarva, Mṛḍa, Rudra, Hara, Śambhu, and Maheśvara— || 17 ||
With these, the wise one should likewise offer the eightfold root mantra;
there is also an oblation of three for Śiva, and the Sviṣṭakṛt offering with the root mantra.
Having thus completed the remainder [of the ritual] as well as the full vessel of water, one with a pure mind should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) one hundred and eight times. (19)
One should sprinkle that water upon one's head with the *pañcabrahma* mantra while experiencing horripilation;
having recited it ten times, one should scatter the water in the various directions.
Having given a sacrificial fee to the Śaivas, one should fetch the *pulaka* for the sake of pacification.
I shall bring you, this Jātavedas, for the protection of the ritual actions of all the Śaivas; I cover you with my bristling body-hairs.
Then, with this mantra, one should cover that fire with *pulakas*;
this covering with *pulakas* is prescribed for the sake of maintaining the fire for three days.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and eat oneself while remaining silent. || 22 ||
Whether within three days, or on the first day,
or on the second, or on the third, having bathed in the morning and wearing white garments, || 23 ||
Wearing a bright white sacred thread and smeared with pure ashes,
one should recite the root mantra and cast off the *pulaka* ashes.
Then, having performed the sixteen services beginning with the invocation,
and having likewise brought forth the Śaiva fire, one should subsequently withdraw it. (25)
The purification of the ashes with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras:
"One should take the excellent ashes with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras;
thereafter, one should wipe them with the subsequent mantra."
Having mixed it with fragrant waters or with the urine of a tawny cow. || 26 ||
Having finely ground together camphor, saffron, musk, ushira root, sandalwood, and the two types of agallochum, [one should prepare the paste].
Then the wise one should take up the large balls with the Praṇava,
and then with the Aghora mantra recited ten times from the root [mantra].
I shall now proclaim another method for the preparation of ash, a concise procedure for preparing the ash:
one should take cow dung with the Sadyojāta mantra and consecrate it with the Vāmadeva mantra. (29)
One should burn the funeral cake with the Aghora mantra, while it should be received with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
it must be diligently worn upon one's own body daily with the Īśāna mantra.
(56) Regarding the threefold nature of ashes:
there are three kinds of ash— pacifying (śāntika), nourishing (pauṣṭika), and that which grants all desires (kāmada).
Cow dung that is connected to its source (the cow) and is grasped by the hand alone.
That which is completely burnt away by Brahma-mantras is here called śāntika. || 31 ||
Having carefully collected cow-dung that has fallen from a cow in the open air, one should then burn it with the six-limbed mantra.
The nourishing rite has been fully described; now hear about that which grants all desires. || 32 ||
When cow dung falls by chance upon a perfectly pure patch of ground, it burns away [impurities] through its grace; thus it is said to be the granter of all desires.
The wearing of ashes produced from the fire of Śiva is recommended for the Śiva-yogins;
likewise, the ashes born of the Virajā fire should be worn by the great sage.
The fire produced from the *aupāsana* rite is distinguished for householders; that produced from the *samit* fire is indeed praised for students (*brahmacārin*s). (35)
For all members of the three [upper] castes, it originates from the *agnihotra* fire;
for *śūdras*, it originates from the cooking fire in the house of a learned *śrotriya*.
This [remedy] arising from the forest fire should also be maintained by all others.
p.
57) The Ritual for the Bath and Smearing with Ashes:
I shall now describe the ritual for the bath with ashes, which destroys the entire multitude of sins.
Having taken up a handful of ashes consecrated with the Saṃhitā-mantras.
One should perform the ash-bath from the head down to the feet. || 37 ||
One should carefully scatter ashes five times on the head with the Īśa mantra;
four times on the mouth with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, and eight times on the heart with the Aghora mantra.
Then again, having diligently rubbed the left foot with the *sadyojāta* mantra eight times, one should likewise [rub] the secret region thirteen times.
One should again perform the smearing of all limbs with ashes while reciting the five Brahma-mantras.
The wearing of ashes is threefold:
smearing (uddhūlana), as well as veiling (avaguṇṭhana), and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra); thus is the wearing of ashes known to be threefold.
Having consecrated it with either the five Brahma-mantras or again with the root mantra,
one who is well-restrained should smear that waterless ash [upon himself].
This smearing of ashes over the entire body from the feet to the crest of the head is known as uddhūlana.
Anointing with consecrated ashes mixed with water is declared to be the "veiling" (avaguṇṭhana); now the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is described.
The wise man should apply the Tripuṇḍra, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, at thirty-two locations by taking [the ash] with the three middle fingers consecrated with the root mantra. (43)
One should likewise apply [the mantras] to thirty-two locations, or sixteen locations, or eight locations, or even five locations. (44)
On the head, on the forehead, on the two ears, on the two eyes, on the nose, the mouth, and the throat, and immediately thereafter on the two shoulders. (45)
At the elbows, the wrists, the heart,
both sides, the navel, the two private parts, the thighs, the buttocks, and the knees.
In the two calves and the two feet, there are thirty-two supreme locations. || 46 ||
The eight-formed Lord, the eight Lords of Knowledge, the world-protectors, and the Vasus are the presiding deities;
a wise person should wear the Tripuṇḍra by means of their names alone.
One should apply [ashes] to sixteen locations; and with a concentrated mind, one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the sixteenth location.
On the head, on the forehead, on the ear, and also on both shoulders. || 48 ||
At the elbows, the wrists, the heart, the sides of the navel,
and the back— at these points during the Pratiṣṭhā [consecration], one should recite the mantra dedicated to their presiding deities.
Śiva, Śakti, Sādākhya, Īśa, and the one called Rudra;
likewise, the two Aśvins are proclaimed as Nāsatya and Dasraka.
And the nine powers beginning with Vāmā—these are the sixteen deities. || 50 ||
Alternatively, [one may place them] on the head, the mouth, the two ears,
as well as the nose, the two arms, the heart, the navel, and likewise on the pair of thighs.
And sixteen [syllables] on the two knees, the two feet, and the back. || 51 ||
Śiva, Skanda, the Moon and Sun, Vighneśa, and Viṣṇu likewise, as well as Śrī in the heart, and Prajāpati in the navel. (52)
Nāgas and nāga maidens, sages and sage-maidens,
as well as the oceans, are remembered to be at his feet, and the sacred fords (tīrthas) are on his back. (53)
Thus, the eight locations—or rather, the sixteen locations—are now described as the eight locations:
the head, the forehead, and immediately after that, the two ears. (54)
The two shoulders, the heart, and the navel—this shall be the eighth.
Brahmā and the seven sages are proclaimed to be the presiding deities. || 55 ||
Alternatively, the forehead, the two arms, the heart, and the navel are declared to be the places for the sacred ash;
the deities there are the five Brahmans.
One should perform [the rite] as far as possible, depending on the place, time, and other factors;
if one is unable even to perform the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana), one should at least apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and so forth.
The procedure for wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra):
the upper mark is the Sāman, the middle mark is the Yajus, and the lower mark is the Ṛc directly; therefore, the triple mark is the triple life-span (triyāyuṣa). || 58 ||
p.
61) One should perform the smearing with all the mantras beginning with "Agniriti," as found in the Jābālopaniṣad, using ashes mixed with water. || 59 ||
The wise, the best of the twice-born, who are righteous and have mastered the Vedas, should always wear the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) with the Tṛyāyuṣa mantra.
Alternatively, the wise student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should, day after day, apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) using ashes mixed with water. (61)
Both the householder and the forest-dweller should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) with the Tṛyambaka mantra, the Praṇava, and the Śiva mantra.
"A mendicant should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the syllable Oṃ uttered three times along with the *saḥ* [praṇava]; this is the teaching of Śiva. (63)
The greatness of the ashes and the fact that the ashes are sacred light have been traditionally declared; by the necessary wearing of them,
one crosses the ocean of worldly existence and enjoys the fruit of absolute liberation.
Merely by wearing the sacred ash, the fruit of all holy places (tīrthas) is attained;
through the wearing of the sacred ash, every sin is reduced to ashes.
This ash is the light of Śambhu; by meditating upon it, the Lord is meditated upon.
Merely by the sight of the ash, one attains the vision of Śiva.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and even great, unbearable diseases flee at the mere sight of the ashes; of this there is no doubt. (67)
For the expulsion of malevolent spirits, the destruction of sins, and the attainment of liberation, there is nothing equal to sacred ash; such is the teaching of Śiva. (68)
The greatness of sacred ash is incalculable; who is able to describe it?
Nevertheless, something has been told; what else do you wish to hear? (69)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Ashes," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the latter portion of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 6 ||
The seventh chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O You who are the support of boundless majesty, resplendent with the ornament of compassion!
I am blessed by the proclamation of the inconceivable greatness of the sacred ash. || 1 ||
O All-pervading Lord, having awakened me to the greatness of the rudrākṣa out of compassion,
please show favor to me, your disciple, O you who are saluted by gods and asuras.
Anantarudra said:
O Lord of Speech, I shall describe to you the nature and the greatness of the Rudrākṣas, according to their origin.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to its retention and its greatness.

In ancient times, for the sake of slaying the three cities (Tripura), the all-pervading Lord Śambhu kept his eyes wide open for a thousand divine years; from that [tears] the origin of the Rudrākṣa [beads] occurred.
From both of her beautiful eyelashes, drops of water fell;
those very drops became great rudrākṣa trees.
They attained the state of being stationary for the sake of showing grace to their devotees. || 5 ||
The greatness of the rudrākṣa:
whatever fruit is obtained by the gift of a cow with its calf to one learned in the Vedas; [that same fruit is obtained from the rudrākṣa].
A person obtains that fruit multiplied a hundred thousand times by merely seeing it. || 6 ||
Furthermore, by touching it, the fruit becomes multiplied ten millionfold;
by wearing it, a person obtains a hundred times ten million merits.
A devoted person obtains merit equal to thousands of lakṣas and crores, as well as hundreds of lakṣas and crores, by the recitation [of mantras] using rudrākṣa beads.
The varieties of Rudrākṣas:
By wearing Rudrākṣas with true devotion, there shall be great fruit.
That which is the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit (dhātrīphala) is declared to be the best. (9)
O Bṛhaspati, know that the medium-sized [liṅga] is said by the wise to be the size of a jujube fruit (badarīphala), while the inferior one is the size of a chickpea (caṇa). 10.
By the command of Śiva, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were born as trees upon the earth, auspicious trees belonging to those respective castes. (11)
The Brāhmaṇas are to be known as white, the Kṣatriyas as red-colored;
the Vaiśyas are to be understood as yellow, and the Śūdras are declared to be black. || 12 ||
A Brāhmaṇa should wear white [garments], but a king (Kṣatriya) should wear red;
a Vaiśya should wear yellow, while a Śūdra should wear black. || 13 ||
Rudrākṣas that are copper-colored, glossy, firm, large, and possessed of thorns are auspicious; those bitten by insects, broken, split, or devoid of thorns are to be avoided.
One should avoid six types of rudrākṣas: those with holes, those that are not round, and those that are defective.
The Rudrākṣa that has its own natural openings is considered the best here;
however, that which is produced through human effort is of middling quality. (15)
The wise man should fasten the strings— equal, smooth, firm, and round— with a linen thread,
ensuring they are uniform across all parts of the body.
That rosary on which a line is clearly visible, like a streak of gold upon a touchstone, should be known as the most excellent; it is to be worn by the worshippers of Śiva. (17)
The places for wearing rudrākṣas and their numbers:
one rudrākṣa on the crest-lock, thirty on the head, thirty-two on the neck, and sixteen on each of the two arms. (18)
(66) One should cause [the breath] to flow for five hundred [breaths] at the wrist and the shoulder;
one should fashion a rosary for the sacrifice of recitation with one hundred and eight [beads]. || 19 ||
One should wear two strings, or three strings, or even five strings,
or even seven strings, around the region of the neck.
In the crown, the earrings, the ear-ornaments, and the necklaces;
in the armlets, the bracelets, and especially in the waist-band.
A man should always wear rudrākṣas while sleeping or drinking. || 21 ||
Three hundred is said to be the lowest, five hundred the middle, and one thousand the highest; thus one should maintain [the practice] according to these divisions.
The wise person should wear Rudrākṣas preceded by the recitation of mantras:
with the Īśāna mantra on the head, with the Tatpuruṣa mantra on the neck,
and with the mantra called Aghora, he should wear them on the hands.
Accompanied by fifty syllables, [one should recite] "Vyomavyāpin" in the belly.
With the five Brahmans as its limbs, the triple-garland consists of five and seven [beads];
or else, one should wear all the beads with the root-mantra. (24)
The Greatness of the Rudrākṣa according to its Different Faces: The single-faced Rudrākṣa is the very nature of the Supreme Reality (paratattva).
By wearing it, one who has conquered the senses merges into that Supreme Reality. (25)
A two-faced rudrākṣa is of the nature of Ardhanārīśvara;
by wearing it, Ardhanārīśvara is eternally pleased with that person.
The three-faced fire itself instantly burns away the sin of killing a woman;
indeed, the three-faced rudrākṣa is declared to be the triple fire.
By retaining that [mantra], the Fire-god is satisfied and clearly grants all desires. || 27 ||
The four-faced rudrākṣa is declared to have the form of Brahmā;
the five-faced rudrākṣa, however, has the nature of the five Brahmās.
The five-faced one is Brahmā himself; he removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Sadāśiva is always satisfied by the mere wearing of it. (29)
The six-faced rudrākṣa has Kārttikeya as its presiding deity and Vināyaka as its presiding deity; it bestows freedom from obstacles and supreme prosperity. (30)
The seven-faced rudrākṣa has the seven mātrās as its presiding deity;
by wearing it, the Mothers, being well-pleased, bestow victory. (31)
The eight-faced rudrākṣa has the lords of the directions as its presiding deities;
it is dear to the eight Vasus, brings joy to Gaṅgā, and is auspicious.
By wearing that, these [deities] become pleased and grant him his desire. || 32 ||
The nine-faced rudrākṣa has the nine Śaktis as its presiding deities;
by the mere wearing of it, the nine Śaktis are pleased. (33)
The ten-faced rudrākṣa is declared to have Yama as its presiding deity;
likewise, there is no doubt that it generates pleasure for him when worn.
The eleven-faced eye has Rudra as its eleven deities;
it is declared to have Indra as its deity and always increases good fortune. || 35 ||
The twelve-faced rudrākṣa has the nature of Mahāviṣṇu,
is presided over by the twelve Ādityas, and increases the delight of the deities.
The thirteen-faced eye is auspicious, granting desires and bestowing purity; by its mere wearing, Kāmadeva becomes propitious. (37)
The eye with fourteen faces, originating from the eyes of Rudra, removes all diseases; one shall always attain perfect health. (38)
They say that its mouth is Rudra, and its bindu is all the deities;
by wearing the rudrākṣa, one is immediately liberated from all sins.
The Determination of Numbers:
With what could the merit of wearing rudrākṣas be compared?
He who, firm in his vows, wears a thousand rudrākṣas—
The gods and demons bow down to him; he is just like Rudra.
In the absence of a thousand [repetitions], however, there should be sixteen on each of the two arms;
one on the topknot; and twelve on each of the two hands. (41)
There are thirty-two [pores] in the region of the throat, six in each of the two ears,
one hundred and eight in the chest, and forty on the head.
Whoever wears a rudrākṣa is always worshipped like Rudra himself.
Wearing Rudrākṣas along with pearls and other gems:
"He who wears Rudrākṣas together with pearls, coral, crystal, silver, lapis lazuli, and gold—he is Rudra; there is no doubt about this. (43)
Even he who wears only rudrākṣas and the mudrās of Rudra is not touched by sins, just as darkness cannot touch the sun.
(p. 70) The Greatness of Rudrākṣa:
A mantra recited with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows infinite fruit.
For men, a recitation performed without rudrākṣa beads yields only that much fruit. || 45 ||
On whose body there is not even a single rudrākṣa, which bestows great merit.
His birth would be as meaningless as one devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). || 46 ||
The wise man who places a rudrākṣa on his head and bathes obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt. || 47 ||
Whoever worships a rudrākṣa after performing an ablution with water certainly obtains that very same fruit which is gained from the worship of a liṅga. || 48 ||
O sinless one, I have described some of the boundless greatness of the rudrākṣa;
it must be guarded with great effort. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Rudrākṣas," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the glorious Candrajñānāgama. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O treasury of unsurpassed knowledge, O ocean of the nectar of supreme bliss!
It has flowed forth like nectar from the lotus-face of the Illustrious One. || 1 ||
Having heard here this unsurpassed majesty of the rudrākṣas, I am satisfied and overcome; I am blessed, O you who are praised by the gods.
Having taught the ritual procedure and the loftiness of the majesty of the illustrious Pañcākṣara as well, look upon me with a glance of compassion and grant me your grace. (3)
Anantarudra said:
Now I shall describe to you, in due order, the essential nature, the majesty, and the procedure for the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) of the great five-syllabled mantra.
The nature and majesty of the five-syllabled mantra:
first, the word *namaḥ* should be employed, and after that, *śivāya*.
This very five-syllabled knowledge (*pañcākṣarī vidyā*) has descended from all the Vedas and Śiva.
In brief, she is the seed of the entire collection of sounds;
first uttered from the mouth of Śiva, she is the self-designator of that very [Śiva].
Resembling molten gold, with full and elevated breasts,
four-armed, three-eyed, and having the crescent moon as her crest-ornament. (7)
Holding a lotus and a blue water-lily, she is serene, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
she is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament. (8)
Seated in the perfected lotus posture with dark, curly hair—this [mantra], preceded by the *praṇava*, is called the six-syllabled one (*ṣaḍakṣarī*). || 9 ||
This six-syllabled mantra should be recited daily by the twice-born preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ);
by women and Śūdras it should be recited with "namas" at the end, without the *praṇava*.
Regarding the Nyāsa of the Seers and others: Vāmadeva is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is said to be its meter (chandas);
Śiva himself is the deity, and the Praṇava is called the seed-syllable (bīja).
Umā is declared to be the Śakti, and the ritual placement (nyāsa) is likewise performed with the six syllables.
Having meditated upon and worshipped the Supreme Lord— either mentally or externally—
one should perform the recitation with diligence, while contemplating the Three-eyed Lord together with Ambā.
One should recite the mantra a thousand times, or half of that, or even a hundred times;
he who performs this daily is indeed Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt. (13)
The description of her colors and so forth:
her fivefold colors are yellow, white, red, green, and blue, appearing as circles of shimmering rays. (14)
If these are separately conjoined and adorned with Bindu and Nāda—the Bindu having the form of a half-moon and the Nāda having the form of a lamp-flame—[then the result follows]. (15)
O best of gods, they say the faces of the five Brahmās are their abodes;
starting from the east and ending with the zenith, they correspond respectively to the letters beginning with *na*. (16)
One should know its other names to be Mūla, Vidyā, Śiva, Sūtra, and likewise Pañcākṣara;
Oṃkāra is considered its heart.
The components of the mantra are as follows:

the letter *na* is said to be the head (*śiras*), while the letter *ma* is called the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Similarly, the letter *śi* is the armor (*kavaca*), and the letter *vā* is called the eye (*netra*). (18)
Just as the syllable *ya*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*,
and also *phaṭ* constitute the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of mantras among the phonemes, so it is here.
The color, the deity, as well as the power, the support, and the meter;
the seer, the location, the Brahman-mantra, and likewise the weapon. || 20 ||
Kalā, Guṇa, Cakra, Prakāśa, Karaṇa, as well as Vāyu and Jñānendriya—these sixteen have been declared in their proper sequence. (21)
The letter Na possesses sixteen forms:
the letter Na is yellow in color, Brahmā is its presiding deity (adhidaivata), Sāvitrī is said to be its power (śakti), and likewise, Earth is its support (ādhāra). || 22 ||
Likewise, the Vāsiṣṭha ṛṣi is indeed joined with the Anuṣṭubh meter;
the western face is Sadyojāta, which belongs to Brahmā.
The weapon is said to be the thunderbolt alone, and the digit (kalā) is indeed cessation (nivṛtti);
the quality (guṇa) is said to be hardness alone, and the discus is four-cornered.
The light of the blazing fire and the mind alone,
when conjoined with the vital breath, become the sense organ of smell, which is a faculty of cognition.
Thus, among these sixteen, the syllable *na* is spoken. || 25 ||
The letter *ma* possesses sixteen forms:
