the letter *ma*, the form of water, the deity Viṣṇu, as well as Lakṣmī, who is declared to be the power (*śakti*), and the support, which is indeed water. (26)
The Triṣṭubh meter is joined with Viśvāmitra as the seer;
the northern face is indeed the Brahman, Vāmadeva. (27)
The weapon is said to be the lotus itself, joined with the kalā called Pratiṣṭhā;
the quality (guṇa), however, is conjoined with fluidity, while the discus is the half-moon of nectar. (28)
The manifestation of Soma itself is the instrument, and the intellect (buddhi) likewise;
conjoined with the apāna wind, the tongue becomes the organ of knowledge.
Thus, the syllable "M" is said to consist of these sixteen [vowels]. || 29 ||
The sixteen-fold nature of Śikāra: Śikāra is indeed of the form of fire, and Rudra is its presiding deity (adhidaivata).
It is conjoined with the power (śakti) of Gaurī, and it is both the support and fire itself. (30)
It is joined with the Uṣṇik meter, with Jamadagni as the seer;
its location is on the right, its face is Aghora, and it is indeed Brahman.
The weapon is said to be the svastika, and its name is Vidyā;
its quality is conjoined with radiance, and its form is a wheel with eight spokes. || 32 ||
The light of the lightning is its manifestation, while I am its instrumental cause and its form;
joined with the vyāna breath, it becomes the eye, the organ of knowledge.
Thus, among these sixteen, the syllable Śi is said to be the letter of the eye. || 33 ||
The letter *vā* possesses sixteen forms; the letter *vā* is the form of Vāyu, whose presiding deity is Īśvara.
Ambikā is the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), and Vāyu is indeed the support. (34)
(76) Endowed with the Bṛhatī meter, the seer is Kāśyapa;
its direction is said to be facing east, and that Brahman is the Puruṣa. || 35 ||
The weapon is of the form of a drop (bindu), as well as the digit (kalā) Śānti;
the quality (guṇa) is said to be touch (sparśa), and this is indeed the six-cornered wheel (ṣaḍaśracakra). || 36 ||
The light of the sapphire shall be the mind,
while the organ [of touch] shall be the skin conjoined with the udāna breath.
Thus, the syllable "vā" is said to consist of these sixteen [elements]. || 37 ||
The sixteen-fold nature of the letter *ya*:
The letter *ya* is the form of space (*vyoma*), its deity is Sadāśiva, it is said to be the power (*śakti*) of Unmanī, and it is called the support, the space. (38)
One should know that it is joined with the Jagatī meter, has Bharadvāja as its seer (ṛṣi), and its position is facing upwards; it is Brahman and Īśāna himself. || 39 ||
The weapon is indeed the trident (śūla), and the digit (kalā) is Śāntyatītā;
the quality (guṇa) is indeed void (śūnya), like the light of a moonstone. (40)
The instrument (karaṇa) is said to be the primordial nature (prakṛti) and also the equalizing breath (samāna-vāyu);
the ear is said to be the organ of cognition—thus these sixteen [principles] are enumerated in order.
The syllable "ya" is said to have neither been in the past nor will it be in the future. || 41 ||
The arising of the five syllables:
"The single Pradhāna alone is traditionally known as the five syllables."
Through the application for the accomplishment of desired objects, direct perception becomes fivefold. || 42 ||
Then the arrangement (prastāraka) is declared; it consists of one hundred and twenty.
In this way, the origin of the five-syllable [mantra] is obtained from the mouth of the Guru. (43)
Mantra is said to be fivefold and action eightfold;
in the Supreme, there is the subsequent arising of the five, which again dissolves back into that very same place.
The seven crores of great mantras, appearing in manifold forms through various faces, dissolve back into the five-syllable mantra and emerge from it once again. (45)
O Bṛhaspati, that which is devoid of knowledge, devoid of ritual action, devoid of faith, unrecited,
and lacking a sacrificial fee— such recitation is always fruitless.
This mantra, which yields great fruit, is accomplished through command, accomplished through ritual action, accomplished through faith, and likewise accomplished through sacrificial fees.
The Procedure for Puraścaraṇa:

Having first received the mantra and the command from the Guru following initiation, one who is composed should form a formal resolve and perform the recitation daily, preceded by the rite of Puraścaraṇa. || 48 ||
One should recite this daily for as long as one lives, eight hundred and more times; by becoming intent on the practice and abstaining from food, one attains the supreme goal.
One who recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with devotion, multiplied fourfold,
while being moderate in diet and self-restrained, is known as a *pauścaraṇika*. (50)

Furthermore, for one who has performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) and becomes a constant reciter [of the mantra], there is no equal in the world; he is perfected and becomes a bestower of perfection.
The procedure for the recitation of mantras:
having performed one's ablutions and having assumed a beautiful seat in a pure place,
one should meditate upon Śaṅkara in the heart, as well as upon one’s own guru and his gurus.
Facing either east or north, observing silence and with a one-pointed mind,
he should purify the five elements by means of burning, flooding, and other such rites.
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth, with his body thus made complete (*sakalīkṛta*),
he should restrain his inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*) and meditate upon the God together with the Goddess.

Having recollected the knowledge, the locus, the vowel, the form, the seer, the meter, the presiding deity, the seed-syllable, the power, and likewise the expressed meaning, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra. (55)
Recitation is said to be of three kinds: the mental is declared the highest, the whispered the middling, and the vocal the lowest; such is the teaching of Śiva. (56)

When one recites the mantra with speech, using words that are high-pitched, low-pitched, or circumflex, with distinct syllables and clear words, this is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa). || 57 ||
That which is uttered with only slight movement of the tongue, heard by oneself but not heard by others, is called *upāṃśu* (whispered). (58)

When, through the intellect, one repeatedly contemplates the meaning of words by moving from syllable to syllable and from word to word via a sequence of imperishable sounds, that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa). || 59 ||

The whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold, while the mental recitation is declared to be a thousandfold; that which includes the internal visualization (sagarbha) is said to be one hundred times more than that.

80) Recitation accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma) is of two kinds: with seed-syllables (sagarbha) and without seed-syllables (agarbha); that which is joined with prāṇāyāma is called recitation with seed-syllables (sagarbha-japa).
Indeed, recitation devoid of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is called "without the embryo" (agarbha). || 61 ||
One should perform forty rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
however, one who is incapable of [reciting] the mantra, its meaning, or the ritual procedure, should recite it according to their capacity.
One should perform five, three, or even one breath control (prāṇāyāma), whether it be "without seed" (agarbha) or "with seed" (sagarbha); however, that which is "with seed" is praised.
Recitation performed with meditative concentration is said to be a thousand times more effective than even that which is done while pregnant [with worldly thoughts].
Among these five types, recitation should be performed according to one's capacity.
The difference in the fruit of recitation according to the finger and other means: Reciting by counting on a single finger is said to yield one unit of merit;
by using a line, one should know it is eightfold; and with *putrajīva* seeds, it is ten times more. (65)
A hundredfold [merit] is gained with conch gems; a thousandfold with corals;
ten thousandfold with crystals; and it is said to be a hundred thousandfold with pearls.
With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [of recitations] are performed; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million (koṭi).
With knots of kuśa grass and rudrākṣa beads, infinite fruit is said to be attained.
A rosary made of thirty beads is a giver of wealth when used in the practice of recitation.
With twenty-seven syllables, it becomes a bestower of nourishment. || 68 ||
When made with twenty-five beads, it bestows liberation;
when made with fifteen beads, it yields the fruit of malevolent magic (abhicāra).
One should know that the thumb bestows liberation, the index finger destroys enemies,
the middle finger grants wealth, and the ring finger indeed brings about peace.
O Lord of Speech, the little finger is said to be used for attracting [others] and in the rite of recitation.
One should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers;
for a recitation performed without the thumb is fruitless.
There is a difference in the fruit according to the distinction of place and so forth:
one should know that recitation performed at home yields an equal result; in a cow-pen it becomes a hundredfold;
likewise, in a sacred forest or a grove, it is said to be a thousandfold. (72)
Ten thousandfold on a beautiful mountain, a hundred thousandfold by a river is declared;
one should know it to be ten millionfold in a temple, and infinite in the presence of Śiva. (73)
O Guru, if one beholds one's chosen *liṅga* situated as the supreme object in the left hand while reciting [mantras], it is impossible for me to describe the fruit thereof.
Recitation is commended in the presence of the sun, fire, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, brahmins, and cows. (75)
One should know that facing east brings subjugation, facing south brings malevolent rites, facing west bestows wealth, and facing north brings peace.
At the time of recitation, one should avoid [the following]:
wearing a turban, wearing a tunic, being naked, having disheveled hair, having the neck covered, having hands without the purificatory ring (pavitra), being impure, or reciting while lamenting. (77)
One should avoid anger, intoxication, hunger, drowsiness, spitting, yawning, and the sight of dogs and low-born persons during the practice of recitation.
If they are available, one should sip water (ācamana) and remember the three-eyed Lord together with Ambā;
or else, one should gaze upon the luminaries or perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 79 ||
Whether eating, lying down, walking, or even standing up,
one should recite the mantra while in a dark place or on an inauspicious road.
One should not recite with the feet extended, nor while in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana),
nor while mounted on a vehicle or a bed, nor when distracted by anxious thoughts.
One who always practices right conduct, offers oblations, and meditates attains what is auspicious. || 81 ||
(83) I shall speak another secret; listen to this which must be concealed.
It must not be told to just anyone, nor to an atheist, nor to a beast. (82)
The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra [is such that] for one devoid of virtuous conduct, for an outcaste, or even for a fallen person,
there is no protection greater than the five-syllabled mantra in the Kali age. (83)
Whether walking or standing, whether performing actions according to one's own will, and whether impure or pure, this mantra is never fruitless. (84)
For men who behave improperly and whose six paths are impure,
this mantra is not fruitless even if it has not been formally imparted by a Guru.
Even for one born of the lowest caste, for the dull-witted, the foolish, the fallen,
the lawless, or the base, this mantra is not fruitless.
For one who possesses devotion toward me, even if they have fallen into every possible state, this will certainly be accomplished; there is no doubt, but it is not so for anyone else.
This Great Mantra shall never at any time become an enemy to anyone—
whether it be a Siddha, a Susiddha, or a Sādhya.

One who is instructed by a perfected (siddha) guru is called "well-perfected" (susiddha); or even one given by an unperfected (asiddha) guru is "perfected" (siddha), while [one given by a guru who is himself] merely "to be accomplished" (sādhya) is likewise [merely] "to be accomplished. (89)
Whether unaccomplished or already accomplished, this succeeds without a doubt for one who possesses an excess of faith toward Śiva, the mantra, and likewise the guru. (90)
Therefore, having abandoned other mantras, one should take refuge in the five-syllabled vidyā; for she protects from the lack of qualification.
A wise person should take refuge in the supreme vidyā, the heart-pleasing five-syllabled one. (91)
Even when other mantras have been mastered, this mantra may not succeed;
yet, once this great mantra is mastered, even they become successful.
The boundless majesty of the great mantra of the five syllables of Śiva cannot be fully described even by Brahmā; it has been stated by me, O sinless one, only in brief. 93.
Conclusion of the Section on the Eight Obstacles:
Indeed, this great set of eight obstacles to Śiva-initiation is renowned throughout all branches of knowledge, and each one individually bestows liberation. (94)
This has been spoken out of affection for you and with the desire to protect the world, O Teacher of the host of gods;
what else do you wish to hear? (95)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Five Syllables," in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Śivaśāsana*, within the dialogue between Ananta Rudra and Bṛhaspati in the latter portion of the *Śrīcandrajñānāgama*.
The Ninth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Knower of the essence of the meaning of all scriptures, O You who are devoted to compassion for all beings, O Infinite Rudra awakened by the desire to uplift the world, salutations be unto You!
Having heard here from the mouth of the illustrious one the greatness of the eight enclosures as proclaimed by infinite scripture, I have attained supreme satisfaction.
Having understood from me the true nature of the five codes of conduct (ācāras),
please favor me with your grace, O you who are saluted by gods and asuras.
Anantarudra said:
[Regarding] the description of the fivefold conduct:
the conduct of the *liṅga*, the conduct of the virtuous, and likewise the conduct of Śiva.
The conduct of servants and the conduct of the assembly—these are proclaimed as the five types of conduct. || 4 ||
"There is indeed no destiny on the surface of the earth other than that which is granted by the Guru through the *liṅga*";
such contemplation of this conviction is called the practice of the *liṅga*. || 5 ||
The daily gratification of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama with wealth acquired through righteous means is known as right conduct (sadācāra). || 6 ||
Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman, devoted to the fivefold cosmic functions;
there is no other goal than Him—this indeed is proclaimed as the conduct of Śiva (śivācāra).
(87) Not listening to the censure of Śiva, of a devotee of Śiva, or of those who follow the Śiva-dharma and so forth— this is called the conduct of the Gaṇas.
All devotees of Śiva are the most excellent on the surface of the earth;
that "I am their servant" is what is known as the conduct of a servant. (9)
O best of gods, there is another method regarding these five modes of conduct mentioned here; I shall explain that as well, so listen. (10)
1. Conduct of the Liṅga:
First, I shall proclaim the conduct of the Liṅga, the abode of auspiciousness, which consists of the forms contained within the initiations known as Kriyā, Vedha, and Mantra.
And the twenty-one initiations are known as the "conduct of the linga" (liṅgācāra). || 11 ||
Initiation is of seven kinds:
that which is comparable to a command, the consecration by means of jars,
and thereafter the mounting upon the svastika, the investiture with the sacred thread, and that which is dependent [upon the teacher].
"Dependent on oneself"—these seven are considered to be the intermediate initiations (dīkṣās) beginning with action (kriyā). || 12 ||
Samaya, asaṃsāra, tattva, jñāna, anugraha, adhyātma, and śuddhavidyā are remembered as the seven internal piercing-points (vedhāntaras). || 13 ||
Firmness in vows, non-violence, the offering of the five senses to him,
the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, and constant delight in the supreme reality. (14)
When the mind is dissolved into the *liṅga*, there is immediate and eternal liberation.
Thus, initiation is said to be of seven kinds, with the initiation by means of mantra being among them. (15)
2. Right Conduct: I shall proclaim right conduct; listen with an attentive mind.
Right conduct alone serves as an ornament for all.
A person devoid of proper conduct is censured in the world. || 16 ||
Maheśvara is pleased by knowledge conjoined with right conduct;
therefore, one who possesses knowledge should be observant of conduct until the fall of the body. 17.
Devotion to Śiva is the foundation for all embodied beings;
conduct is the supreme dharma, and conduct is the supreme wealth. (18)
If knowledge is devoid of right conduct, it does not lead to success.
Listen: in that regard, right conduct consists of eightfold character (śīla). (19)
In the context of right conduct, the eightfold ethical discipline (*śīla*) should be known as the first sprout; that which has arisen is the second;
the two-fold leaf is the third; and the fully grown state is the fourth. (20)
The fifth [stage] is with the trunk; the sixth is said to be with the branches;
the seventh should be known as with the flowers; and the eighth would be with the fruit. (21)
The wish-fulfilling tree of virtuous conduct, enriched with the eightfold discipline and well-cultivated, bestows great desired fruits upon the noble-minded who possess true devotion. (22)
I shall briefly explain the seed-nature known as the "Sprout," which is characterized by the sprout and other [stages] of moral conduct;
it is beautified by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), endowed with the compassion of the Guru.
The notion that one's own body is material is called the "sprout" (aṅkura). || 23 ||
The wise should accept as "innate character" (śīla) that which arises from one's own dwelling together with wife and others who have been initiated. (24)
Indeed, the constant and diligent wearing of the marks of the Śaivas, such as ashes and the like, is called the "two-fold conduct" (dvidala-śīla). || 25 ||
The constant contemplation of the greatness of the Śiva-dharmas is called "increased conduct" (pravṛddha-śīla); it is taught that this increases devotion. (26)
That one remains without food without having first worshipped the chosen emblem (liṅga) should be understood as this "stem" of conduct, which is a means for cultivating devotion. (27)
The non-appropriation of any substance not offered to the desired deity is indeed what is called "conduct" (*śīla*) together with its branches; this must be observed by those intent on devotion. (28)
The avoidance of discarding that which has been offered as grace (prasāda) to Śiva is called "virtue with flowers" (sapuṣpa-śīla); this should be known as the highest form. || 29 ||
The contemplation of the Guru, the *jaṅgama-liṅga*, and the [static] *liṅga* as one is called "fruitful conduct" (*saphala-śīla*); it is supreme and brings about immediate accomplishment.
He who, steadfast in devotion, constantly practices the eightfold right conduct, attains immediate perfection through the grace of Śambhu. (31)
3. Śivācāra:
O Sage, listen attentively as I describe the conduct of Śiva, which consists of the purification of sixteen items, including substances, locations, and dwellings.
That which is practiced according to the path taught in the Śiva-śāstras is known as Śivācāra. || 32 ||
There are sixteen types of purification.

Food already in the hand [of the giver], or that which has been purified by means of ash, as well as fruits, roots, and so forth, may be accepted; this is considered the purification of substances (dravya-śuddhi). || 33 ||

A sacred field (kṣetra) adorned with stone, wood, and other materials marked with the Nandi-mudrā should be accepted by those devoted to it; this is proclaimed as the purification of the field (kṣetraśuddhi).
Whether it be constructed by devotees or even merely marked with the Śiva-liṅga, a house should be accepted by devotees; this is declared to be the purification of the home. (35)
Or even a collection of vessels made by a devotee, or marked with the Śiva-liṅga, may be accepted;
this is proclaimed as the purification of vessels. (36)
Grass and other such items brought by devotees, or those purified with ashes, may be accepted; this is declared to be "purity by grass" (tṛṇaśuddhi).
Wood brought with devotion or consecrated with ritual power (vibhūti) should be accepted by those observing the vow; this is declared to be the purification of the wood. (38)
Whether by means of ash produced in the garden of devotees and consecrated, or by means of sacred ash (vibhūti) prepared through the practice of devotees; || 39 ||
Betel leaf accompanied by areca nut and lime-powder should indeed be accepted by the devotees; this is declared to be the purification of the betel-roll (vīṭikā).
Food cooked by those endowed with Śiva-initiation, which has not been looked upon by non-devotees, should be accepted by devotees; this is considered the purity of cooking. (41)
One should avoid buffalo and sheep products such as ghee, curd, milk, and buttermilk;
however, those from cows should always be accepted—this is considered the purification of substances. (42)
(92) Because of the relinquishing of desire-driven actions, which are the cause of rebirth,
the attainment of freedom from birth is called the purification of existence (bhava-śuddhi). || 43 ||
Compassion toward all beings, purification through the five elements, and freedom from harming living beings—this is declared to be the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). (44)
Having completely renounced all desires, the constant contemplation of the state of Śiva by means of the mind is declared to be purity of being at all times. (45)
Just as there should be no injury to ants and other small creatures with one's feet, so should one's walking be carefully attended; this is considered the purification of the path.
When the time prescribed by the scriptures has arrived, and it is silent and pleasant, the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is performed; this is what is called "purity of time" here.
The abandonment of speech that is false, harsh, contemptuous, loathsome, or deceitful is called purity of speech (vāk-śuddhi). || 48 ||
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, or in a social gathering—at all times and in all places—association with virtuous devotees is declared to be the purification of people. (49)
O learned one, this practice of Śiva is concealed in all the scriptures;
by performing it, a mortal attains union with Śiva.
4. The Conduct of the Community (Gaṇācāra).
I shall now describe the conduct of the community, which is the sole means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, the conduct of the Gaṇas was carried out by the hosts of devotees; so it is called.

Regarding the sixty-four rules of conduct, which are supreme among all communal practices and grant immediate accomplishment in the highest [path], there exist these sixty-four rules; listen to them. (52)
In that regard, among the sevenfold precepts,
that which consists in speaking only what is true according to the facts through speech, perfected by devotion—
that truth is said to be the first precept in all the scriptures. (53)
One should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant untruth;
one should speak that which is both pleasant and true—this is called the second virtue. (54)
The daily recitation of the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, which provide the sole awakening to the knowledge of Dharma, is declared to be the third ethical discipline (śīla). (55)
The constant praise of Śiva, of the devotees of Śiva, and especially of the Guru, is called the fourth virtue. (56)
And whatever avoidance of praise from other gods and humans at any time—that is called the fifth precept. (57)
Whenever and wherever one may abandon self-praise, that is said to be the sixth precept, unanimously agreed upon by all the scriptures. (58)
To never engage in reviling or disparaging gods, humans, or those devoid of qualities— this is called the seventh ethical discipline. (59)
Thus, these seven kinds of verbal conduct have been described by me;
now listen as I shall explain that conduct which pertains to the hands.
The fivefold morality pertaining to the hand consists of the prostration performed toward the preceptor, the living beings, and the emblems;
this is declared as the eighth morality, as taught by all the scriptures. (61)
The constant procurement of all requisites for worship day and night is called the ninth discipline, the sole cause for pleasing Śiva. (62)
The daily recitation of the root mantra with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads every day is declared to be the tenth virtue, which purifies all sins. (63)
The daily worship of the Guru, of the devotees of Maheśvara, and of the Beloved of Bhavānī—this is remembered as the eleventh habit. (64)
Giving gifts according to one's ability out of devotion to the Guru, to living beings, and for the sake of the Śiva-dharma is called the twelfth virtue, śīla.
Thus, the fivefold morality connected with the hands has been described.
Now I shall speak of the morality pertaining to the feet, which destroys the flood of evil. (66)
(95) There is fourfold conduct pertaining to the feet: namely, that which consists in approaching the Guru who is a devotee of Maheśvara.
That was declared as the thirteenth by Śambhu, the all-knowing one.
The circumambulation performed even for the Guru who is a devotee of Maheśvara, done with a state of devotion, is declared to be the fourteenth. (68)
Indeed, because of the devotee's constant desire to procure the various requisites for worship, that [set of qualities] is considered the fifteenth. (69)
For the purpose of worshipping even the Guru who possesses the desired *liṅga*, there is a firm seat;
that is called the "sixteenfold" by the trident-bearing God of gods. (70)
Thus, the fourfold morality pertaining to the feet has been described.
Therefore, I shall speak of that which is connected to the skin; listen to it with careful attention. (71)

The conduct that is eternally connected to the skin— namely, the constant touching of the desired linga without separation— is declared to be seventeenfold, serving as the basis for the meaningfulness of the body. (72)
Adorned with the horripilation produced by the touch of the desired Liṅga, this is declared to be the eighteenth virtue, which destroys worldly existence. (73)
This morality connected with the skin is proclaimed to be of two kinds;
I shall now describe that which pertains to the eyes—listen to it with attentiveness. (74)
The virtue residing in the eye is tireless and full of affection, consisting in the gazing upon the beloved's form.
The nineteenfold morality has been declared as the destroyer of the fear of existence. (75)
The emergence of tears of joy arising from the sight of the desired Linga is clearly declared as the twentieth discipline by the one who bears the crescent moon upon his crest. (76)
Thus, these two kinds of conduct connected with the eyes have been described.
Now I shall speak of that pertaining to the tongue; listen, endowed with faith. (77)
The conduct pertaining to the tongue, which consists of tasting the flavors offered with faith every day, is said to be twenty-one-fold; now hear that which pertains to the nose. (78)
The morality pertaining to the nose is the smelling of fragrances such as those from withered flower garlands;
this is declared to be the twenty-second. Now, listen to that pertaining to the ear. (79)
The moral conduct heard from the Guru Śiva, and the daily listening to the hymns of his devotees—
these twenty-three are declared to be the cause for attaining liberation. (80)
Indeed, listening to the censure of the devotees of the Guru Śiva is declared to be the twenty-fourth; now hear from me regarding the physical [sins]. || 81 ||
(97) Bodily morality arises solely through the grace of the Guru, who possesses the desired marks and wanders as a mendicant.
For this purification of the body is indeed the twenty-fifth precept.
And the restraint of the senses from prohibited objects is called the twenty-sixth virtue, which wards off the defects of worldly existence. (83)
Upon touching an object that should not be touched, purification occurs through bathing with water or ash;
indeed, this constitutes the twenty-seventh form of purity, while virtuous conduct (*śīla*) is the prevention of faults.
Avoiding sitting, lying down, or socializing with those who are not kinsmen—this twenty-eighth precept is taught as a means for achieving purity. 85.
The constant wearing of sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, and lingas upon the body—this is the twenty-ninth discipline, the sole means for achieving the path to liberation. 86.
The physical [discipline] has been declared to be fivefold, the sole means for attaining liberation.
Now I shall speak of the mental; listen with a single-minded focus on ethical conduct (śīla). 87.

Mental morality is the avoidance of intentional thought regarding objects of prohibited enjoyment; for that is the morality of celibacy (brahmacarya) as enjoined by the Lord in the thirty[-first chapter]. 88.
(98) One may indeed cultivate devotion toward [virtuous] objects, but never toward improper objects;
this thirty-first ethical discipline is proclaimed as freedom from desire. 89.
One should restrain anger toward unrighteousness, but never toward enemies;
this thirty-second virtue, non-anger, is the means to liberation. 90.
One should not harbor excessive greed for wealth and such; rather, one should cultivate it toward the worship of Śiva.
This is proclaimed as the thirty-third virtue, known as non-greed (alobha).
One should not harbor delusion toward one's devotees, nor toward one's wife or children;
this is proclaimed as the thirty-fourth virtue, known as non-delusion (amoha).
One should never harbor envy toward the instruments [of practice] themselves;
this virtue of non-envy is proclaimed as the thirty-fifth. (93)
One should not give way to pride in victory through illusion, nor in dharma, nor even in prosperity.
This discipline, called "freedom from pride," is proclaimed as the thirty-sixth.
The abandonment of the investigation into the virtues and faults of the Guru while practicing [his service] is declared to be the thirty-seventh moral conduct, which bestows the fruit of merit. (95)
That which consists in not causing harm to any living being whatsoever is declared to be this thirty-eighth virtue, known as non-violence (ahiṃsā). || 96 ||
The inability to endure the sight of suffering in living beings is what is termed compassion (*dayā*); this well-known ethical discipline (*śīla*) is proclaimed as the thirty-ninth. (97)
Whether in action or in speech, that which arises from another or even from oneself—
this is declared as *hrīyā-śīla* (the discipline of modesty) by the Trident-bearer as the fortieth [virtue].
The avoidance of partiality toward both enemy and one's own son is declared to be the forty-first virtue, known as uprightness (ārjava). 99.
Faith in the Āgamas and the Nigamas, as well as in that which is spoken by the Guru—
this is the virtue called śraddhā (faith), declared as the forty-second.
The non-avoidance of the Dharma even when faced with a terminal crisis—this is proclaimed as the forty-third virtue, known as fortitude. || 101 ||
The absence of malice even toward those who are enemies and intent on doing harm is the virtue called forbearance; it is declared to be the forty-fourth [virtue]. (102)
The absence of desire for the pursuit of enjoyments within one's mind is the relinquishing of attachment to enjoyments;
this is declared to be the forty-fifth [perfection]. (103)
A state free from negligence in action or in speech—that is *dhairya* (fortitude);
this is determined here as the forty-sixth [type of] conduct (*śīla*). || 104 ||
The complete abandonment of conceptual thoughts directed toward objects other than Śiva is proclaimed as the forty-seventh [perfection], namely, the discipline known as *dama*. (105)
The performance of duties without deficiency and the non-acceptance of another's property is declared to be the forty-eighth virtue, known as non-stealing.
Contentment is the happiness arising from the absence of attachment to objects not yet acquired; know that this constitutes the forty-ninth [factor] of ethical discipline (śīla). 107.
The constant remembrance of the two names and forms of the Supreme Lord, which bestows liberation while living, is declared to be the fifty-fold conduct. (108)
The uninterrupted contemplation of the name, qualities, and so forth of Śambhu is proclaimed as the fifty-first [discipline], namely, *śīla*, which removes the fetters. (109)
Constantly meditating upon the massaging of Śambhu’s feet and so forth—this is declared to be the fifty-two-fold service of the feet. (110)
O Lord of Speech, that mental worship of Śambhu which consists of the invocation and other rites—this is declared to be the fifty-threefold conduct. (111)
Indeed, that mental prostration performed daily at the lotus feet of Śambhu is proclaimed as the fifty-fourth virtuous conduct (śīla). 112.
That which consists of the constant performance of service for Śambhu with the mind is indeed *dāsya*; this is declared to be the fifty-fifth discipline (*śīla*). (113)
Indeed, that contemplation of friendship with Śambhu, whose nature is auspiciousness, is this fifty-sixth discipline known as "friendship. (114)
The surrendering of the entire burden of bondage and liberation is this "Surrender of the Self" (Ātmārpaṇa), which is here prescribed as the fifty-seventh [chapter]. 115.
The constant mental recitation of the root mantra—this is the fifty-eighth discipline that should be observed. (116)
The contemplation of Śambhu’s divine form performed within the heart is proclaimed as the fifty-ninth virtue, known as meditation (dhyāna). || 117 ||
That very state which is maintained without interruption, like a stream of oil, is called *dhāraṇā*; this is declared to be the sixty-first discipline (*śīla*). (118)
The stability of the mind in meditative absorption, like a lamp in a windless place, is called concentration; this is the sixty-first virtue that thoroughly impels [the practitioner]. 119.
Meditating upon the Lord of the Universe with the sense of "I am He," one should contemplate all activities being performed everywhere solely through the medium of those very senses.
That which one practices is called the sixty-two-fold conduct. || 120 ||
O Preceptor of the Gods, that which is called the conduct of the Great Lord— which consists of the continuous pursuit of forms beyond all limits— is declared to be sixty-threefold.
Meditating upon the formless nature of the Lord through his own form,
he forgets even the self as the universe by virtue of the bliss of Śiva.
He who remains steadfast in the sixty-fourfold ethical conduct (śīla) that has been proclaimed; || 122 ||
He who is enriched by the sixty-four virtues is indeed Śiva and none other;
through the yoga of practicing this, one attains union with Śiva.
Thus has the conduct of the community been proclaimed; now hear the conduct of servants.
The conduct of a servant,
the state of servitude, and heroic servitude— the conduct of a servant is considered to be twofold: namely, the performance of service toward the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama.
This state of servitude was thus designated by Śambhu, the God of gods.
Having thus offered his body to the Preceptor (deśika), his mind to Śambhu, and likewise his wealth to the Living Liṅga (jaṅgama), he should be endowed with great enthusiasm. (125)
That which one remains steadfastly desiring only supreme liberation is known as the state of being a hero’s servant (*vīrabhṛtyatva*), the means for attaining Śiva’s grace. (126)
Thus has this determination of the fivefold conduct been told to you;
it is the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, the sole means for attaining liberation. 127.
It should never be taught to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who lacks devotion;
it should not be spoken to one who has no son, nor to one devoid of faith.
It must be guarded with great effort; what do you wish to hear beyond this? || 128 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Fivefold Conduct," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O you who are endowed with all auspicious qualities and adorned by the sons of Kadrū!
O Inner Rudra, awakened by the upliftment of living beings, salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
In the Āgamas, the divisions of the Śaivas are proclaimed in many ways;
in some places four are mentioned, while in others indeed seven.
In some places ten [perfections] are mentioned, while in others they are described differently;
having synthesized those, please explain the equipment here without doubt. (3)
Antarudra said:
"I shall now declare to you the eightfold Śaivas, the unsurpassed classification of the Śaivas."
The first is Anādiśaiva; the second is Ādiśaiva.
The third would be Pūrvaśaiva, and the fourth Miśraśaiva.
The fifth is Śuddhaśaiva, and the sixth is indeed Mārgaśaivaka;
the seventh should be known as Sāmānya, and then the eighth is Vīraśaiva. || 5 ||
1. Now I shall describe the characteristics of that primordial Śaiva [nature] correctly and in due order:
Śambhu is the primordial Śaiva, as are his attendants.
2. The characteristics of the Ādiśaivas: The Ādiśaivas are to be known as the great sages beginning with Kauśika. || 6 ||
Kauśika, Kaśyapa, Bharadvāja, Atri, and Gautama—
these were first consecrated within the five faces of Maheśvara.

For those who have been initiated from the mouth of the Guru—whether they belong to his own lineage or to another lineage—and who observe the Śāmbhava vow according to the procedure taught at the end of the Āgamas; || 8 ||
By means of the three initiations known as Vedha, Anukriyā, and Abhikhyā,
he shines with the three limbs, from which the three Liṅgas manifest.
O Bṛhaspati, they are called the Ādiśaivas on this earth.
Indeed, in the installation of Maheśa, in festivals, in ritual ablutions and the like,
the Ādiśaivas, who are praised by the world, are authorized for the office of preceptor.
3. The Characteristics of the Pūrvaśaivas: Indeed, the Pūrvaśaivas are to be known as the Śiva-brahmins born of unmarried maidens (kānīna);
for they were born from girls who had not yet been wedded, and there are many of them belonging to five lineages (pañcagotra). || 11 ||

Regarding the initiations (dīkṣā) of the Śaivas described here according to their prior nature, those who speak of Śiva are of two kinds, based on whether they accept or do not accept [the external observances]. 12.
Refined by the initiations (dīkṣā) mentioned in the earlier section, they are indeed without external marks (aliṅgin);
for they are authorized to perform sacrifices for their own sake and for the sake of others. || 13 ||
O you who are honored by the gods, for they are authorized to act as priests for the Lord, to perform service for him, and to adorn the temple of Śiva. (14)
For they have no qualification for the office of a teacher or for rituals such as the consecration of images;
indeed, even though these men have been initiated, there is no doubt that this is because of their status as sons of an unmarried woman (kānīna).

(The Characteristics of a Devalaka) Now, those who, being uninitiated, are devoted solely to performing sacrifices for the sake of others are indeed called devalakas; they are censured for all ritual acts. 16.
In a place other than a temple of Śiva, even their touch causes harm;
yet, because they worship Śiva, their status as Śaivas is perfectly clear. (17)
Due to being far removed from the initiation of Śiva, due to consuming the substances of Śiva,
and due to faults such as the loss of faith regarding the sphere of service to Śiva;
O Lord of Speech, they are declared to be the impurities in all the scriptures. (18)
4. The Characteristics of the Mixed Śaiva: Now, O Preceptor of the Gods, listen as I describe the Mixed Śaiva [tradition]:
Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara. (19)
Those who, having seated [the deities] on a single seat, worship them by merging [them together], are indeed called Miśra-Śaivas because of their mixed worship. || 20 ||
For these [others], there shall be neither initiation into Śiva nor the contemplation of Śiva’s supremacy;
their status as Śaivas arises merely from wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads and from the worship of mixed [deities].
Because they possess a state of mixture, they are proclaimed as the Miśra-Śaivas.
Because they are seen to be Śākta within, Śaiva without, and Vaiṣṇava in the midst of the assembly—being thus mixed—they are celebrated as Miśra-Śaivas (Mixed Śaivas). || 22 ||

5. The Characteristic of Pure Śaivism: Therefore, I shall describe the well-known Pure Śaivism, honored by the wise, which consists of the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, according to the ancient initiation (paurāṇadīkṣā).
Having been initiated, their minds were solely intent upon the worship of the Śiva-liṅga alone.
O Bṛhaspati, those who possess faith in the supremacy of Śiva and experience the state of being Śiva are called pure Śaivas on this earth. (24)
6. The Characteristics of Mārgaśaiva: I shall now proclaim the Mārgaśaiva [path], which is the path leading to the proximity of liberation;
it comprises the adoption of the three types of initiation (dīkṣā) as declared in the conclusions of the Vedas and Āgamas.
The perfection of knowledge regarding the six locations and the worship of Śiva at the six times. || 25 ||
One should constantly perform the recitation of the six-syllable mantra twenty-one thousand six hundred times, while contemplating the identity of the [individual] with the Liṅga.
This Dharma, ending with the Mārgaśaiva, was proclaimed by the Lord. || 26 ||
Even though there is equality with the Ādiśaiva regarding the acceptance of initiation and other rites,
[this system] possesses distinguished dharmas that bestow liberation swiftly.
Uninterrupted practice is what is distinguished in the Mārgaśaiva [tradition]. || 27 ||
7. The General Characteristics of Śaivism: I shall now describe general Śaivism; listen to it with careful attention.
All these [sects], beginning with the Śāktas, abide within five systems of thought. (28)
Because they have performed the purification of the paths (*adhvaśodhana*) and have received the *gāyatrī*, they are indeed called "common Śaivas" (*sāmānyaśaiva*) upon this earth. (29)
8. The Characteristics of Vīraśaiva:
I shall proclaim the Vīraśaiva doctrine, which is known from both the Śruti and the Tantras.
It is proclaimed to be of two kinds: Śrauta and Svatantra. || 30 ||
That which is rich in the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life is called Śrauta;
that which is devoid of those duties and is independent is called Svatantra. || 31 ||
The acceptance of the initiations taught in the Uttara-kāṇḍa of the Āgama is the same as that of the Ādi-śaiva; hear now the distinction regarding this matter.
In the event of separation from one's chosen deity or in the failure to maintain one's vows,
the abandonment of life like a blade of grass is considered the *vīravratam* (heroic vow).
An exceptional degree of devotion and enthusiasm is also called heroism (vīratva).
Through the adoption of the heroic vow (vīravrata), it is proclaimed as Vīraśaivism.
Furthermore, the divisions of Vīraśaiva are threefold according to the distinctions of Sāmānya and the rest;
they are threefold as Sāmānya, Viśeṣa, and Nirābhārī.
Now, I shall describe in order the characteristics of these general Vīraśaivas; listen attentively.
Their characteristic is the worship performed through the unification of the three types of liṅgas, beginning with the *iṣṭa*.
One should maintain an equal disposition toward the guru, Maheśvara, and one's own chosen liṅga.
The worship of the *liṅga* three times a day with available materials—
this is proclaimed as the duty of a general Vīraśaiva.
The definition of the Viśeṣavīra-śaiva is as follows:
because of the performance of specific duties, he is indeed distinguished (viśeṣa). || 37 ||
Having fed one devotee of Maheśvara, or two, or three, every day,
he should indeed eat the remnants of that meal without negligence.
And the worship of the Liṅga at the six periods of the day is performed with the obligatory ritual ingredients.
Either the *droṇa* flower, the *bilva* leaf, or even the *karavīra*;
or else flowers such as the *mallikā*, *utpala*, *punnāga*, *jāti*, and others. (39)
Endowed with self-restraint, one should offer one, three, or even two of these;
thus shall I observe these rules until the departure of my life-breath. (40)
"The restraint that is traditionally taught as 'I shall not maintain my life-breaths otherwise'—when joined with such rules as these, it is called a 'special' (viśeṣa) observance. (41)
The characteristics of the *nirābhārī* and the *vīraśaiva*:
one who follows the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*) is called a *nirābhārī*; in the *Svacchanda-tantra*, one who has renounced wife and other attachments is described as a *nirābhārī*. (42)
Independent and free from support,
whether shaven-headed or with matted hair, and endowed with the staff and saffron robes;
In the independent Vīraśaiva tradition, however, the *nirābhārī* should wander the earth.
The Vaidika Nirābhārī is characterized by the topknot (śikhā) and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and possesses a staff (daṇḍa) and ochre-colored garments (kāṣāya-cela);
however, in the Vaidika Vīraśaiva tradition, he is known as a Nirābhārī.
However, the non-separation from one's own chosen *liṅga* is considered equal for both. || 44 ||

Free from appearances, characterized by the universal, devoid of longing, unified with his own true nature, subsisting on alms, free from fear, silent, and endowed with compassion for all beings— he is known as the Nirābhāra (the Supportless One). || 45 ||
Wearing a necklace and a water-pot, endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
and carrying a staff and a loincloth, he is celebrated as "Nirābhārin" (the one who bears nothing).
If one who has reached the stage of Nirābhāra should happen to be present, this stage must be accepted from him, as indeed must the Praṇava. (47)
In the absence of such a place, it should instead be accepted at a temple of Śiva or at the root of a bilva tree, according to the command of the Lord.
Even when the *praṇava*, which consists of the subtle five syllables, is being recited,
the gross five-syllabled mantra of Śiva must never be abandoned by ascetics. (49)

These divisions of Śaivism are distinguished by their engagement with the conduct of vision (darśanācāra) and so forth; likewise, the non-duality of Śiva, characterized by specific distinctions, is the doctrine accepted by the Vedas for the Ādi, the Pūrva, as well as for the Mārga and Vīra [Tantras]. (50)
The doctrine known as Śuddhādvaita (Pure Non-dualism) is considered the imagined (parikalpita) view of Miśra;
this [view] is indeed the qualified (viśiṣṭa) form of Sāmānya’s [doctrine], consisting precisely of the non-duality of Śakti and so forth. (51)
For the hero of the initial path, no funeral rites for the deceased exist;
therefore, cremation and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) are not approved for them. || 52 ||
However, for those such as Pūrva and the others, their state as pretas and the karma resulting from it are indeed distinguished,
because they do not possess the supreme initiation of Śambhu.
Those divisions of the Śaivas are said to have their root in differences of conduct;
yet the Pradhāna alone is the one [reality], endowed with all knowledge.
O best of sages, it is known as the Śaiva [scripture] from which all secondary designations have departed.
When it was adorned by the Śaiva initiations of those resting at the edge of the village, and resplendent with three liṅgas connected to the three ancillary parts; || 55 ||
(113) Rich with the duties of the castes and stages of life, endowed with the knowledge of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*),
distinguished by the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*), and adorned with the five modes of conduct (*pañcācāra*). || 56 ||
This ritual, which brings about the immediate destruction of bonds and is a synthesis of knowledge,
is graced by the office of the preceptor in rites such as the consecration of Maheśvara.
Moreover, this very [reality] is described in various ways in many places;
through its association with particular qualities, it comes to be designated by those respective names. (58)
Because it has circulated through creations since beginningless time, this is called "beginningless"; and because it is the first among all doctrines here, O Lord of Speech, it is so designated.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, it is known in some places as Ādiśaiva.
It is known as Mārgaśaiva because it prioritizes the path to liberation;
it is also called Śuddha (Pure) because it avoids association with other deities.
In some cases, it is called "mixed" (miśra) because of its connection with the rituals prescribed in the Smṛtis;
and it is remembered as "Vīraśaiva" due to its association with the Vīra-vow. || 61 ||
(114) Thus, O Lord of Speech, the various divisions of Śaivism have been correctly expounded by you.
What else do you wish to hear, including the Pradhāna-śaiva? 62.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Division of the Śaivas," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 10 ||
The eleventh chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O wearer of the skeleton, O omniscient one, O death of Death, O ocean of compassion!
O Bhagavān Anantarudra, I bow to you; please show me your grace. || 1 ||
I wish to hear the daily ritual (āhnika) for those Śaivas who are devoted to the Śāmbhava vow and whose selves are disciplined; please describe the procedure in its entirety.
Anantarudra said:
Regarding the daily observance for those steadfast in the Śāmbhava vow:
having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should [visualize] the beloved Liṅga in one's eyes.
Having meditated upon the Lord Śiva together with Ambā while touching him, and having reflected upon the task to be performed.
Regarding the description of pure conduct:
unwearied, one should go to a spot outside the village in the south-eastern direction, at a distance.
Having placed the Śiva-sūtra and the sacrificial thread upon his head and covered it with a cloth,
he should also place his head elsewhere and set down a water vessel.
And having discharged urine and feces, one should perform purification according to the prescribed rule.
Then, endowed with right conduct, he should clean his teeth with the branch of a milk-exuding thorny tree; if tooth-sticks are unavailable, [he should do so otherwise]. (5)
One should cleanse the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water;
then, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one should perform the Vāruṇa bath in a river or similar body of water.
Having performed the Vāruṇa bath and other rites, wearing the sacred thread (upavīta) and having tied his topknot (śikhā), he should enter the water;
then, having established the Śiva-tīrtha, he should perform his bath in its midst.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules with the limbs of Śiva-Brahman and the limbs of Vidyā,
one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva.
Having then satiated the gods and others, he should withdraw the *śivatīrtha* water;
then, having discarded his wet garment, he should put on two washed garments.
Having immersed oneself and taken the desired liṅga,
one should then take the sacred ash and perform the ash-bath for the removal of all defects.
One should perform the smearing of all limbs with dry white ashes,
and then one should envelop all the limbs with those same ashes mixed with water. (11)
Then, with consecrated ashes mixed with water, one should indeed apply the *tripuṇḍra* marks upon thirty-two locations, starting from the root [of the hair].
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the head,
the forehead, the two ears, the two eyes, as well as on the nose, the mouth, the neck, and the two shoulders; || 13 ||
At the elbows, the wrists, the heart, both sides, the navel, the two private parts, the thighs, the buttocks, and the knees; || 14 ||
Having likewise applied the three lines (tripuṇḍra) on the two calves and the two feet— these being the thirty-two supreme locations— one should thereafter wear rudrākṣa beads.
One should perform the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana), attending to the two twilights with the Sāvitrī as the root mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual worship (arcā) belonging to the time of dawn.
Having recited the Sāvitrī, the well-known mother of all mantras,
one should then worship Mahādeva, who resides within the orb of the sun.
One should also recite the six-syllabled mantra with a concentrated mind, as prescribed.
Facing either the east or the north, one should meditate upon the God and the Goddess, as well as one's own Guru; thereafter, one should mutter the eight names. (18)
The Eight Names of Śiva:
Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Śambhu, Umāpati, Saṃsāravaidya, Sarvajña, and Paramātman—this is the octet. (19)
Afterwards, having washed both hands and smeared them with sandalwood paste,
one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), preceded by the purification of the hands.
The ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) and so forth is considered threefold, known as maintenance (*sthiti*), origination (*utpatti*), and dissolution (*laya*).
For householders, the placement is that of maintenance; for celibate students (*brahmacārin*), it is that of origination.
And for ascetics and forest-dwellers, the withdrawal of the ritual placement (saṃhṛtinyāsa) is prescribed.

Likewise, the placement for withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa) is said to be for a married woman; for a maiden it is said to be the placement for origination (utpatti), and for a consecrated virgin (suvāsinī) it should be the placement for maintenance (sthiti).
The placement [of mantras] from the thumb to the little finger is known as *sthitinyāsa*;
likewise, it is performed starting from the right thumb and ending with the left thumb.
The placement [of mantras] during emanation has been explained; that which is the reverse is the dissolution. || 23 ||
One should indeed assign the letters beginning with *na* along with their nasal bindus in sequence;
having assigned Śiva to the fingers, one should also assign him to the palms and the backs of the hands.
Then one should perform the placement of weapons (astranyāsa) in the ten directions with the weapon-mantras.
Meditation on the Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti:
Furthermore, the five Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti consist of the five elements;
they should be properly meditated upon together with their respective insignia and the lords of the five elements. (25)

One should contemplate the five-syllabled Vidyā in the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and at the aperture of Brahmā; one should recite it for the purpose of purifying those [channels]. (26)
Having restrained the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), one should then accomplish a body consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya) according to the number of the qualities (guṇas);
thereafter, one should sever the knot of the elements (bhūtagranthi) with the Astra-mantra and the Astra-mudrā.
One should unite the self, impelled by the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) through the suṣumṇā channel and emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), with the splendor of Śiva.
And having dried the body with the wind, one should burn it with the fire of time.
Having performed the immersion in nectar for that [body] which has indeed been reduced to ashes,
one should then contemplate that a body consisting of vidyā has arisen. (29)
Then, one should join the Self— which has emerged from Śiva in the form of a lamp flame— to that body composed of knowledge through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having meditated upon him as having entered the intermediate body within the heart-lotus,
one should again sprinkle that body composed of knowledge with a shower of nectar.
One should again perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), preceded by the purification of the hands;
thereafter, one should perform the placement on the body (dehanyāsa) and the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) according to the prescribed rule.
Then one should perform the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa) upon the joints of the hands, feet, and so forth;
thereafter, having performed the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga), one should then carry out the binding of the directions (digbandha).
Having thus performed the purification of the body and self by means of this summary,
and having attained the state of Śiva, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva. (34)
Now, regarding other methods of ritual placement (nyāsa):
he who has the opportunity for them, or whose mind is free from confusion,
should perform the rite of placement according to the extensive procedure.
Therein, first is the placement of the Mātṛkās (Mātṛkā-nyāsa), followed by the placement of Brahman (Brahma-nyāsa);
third is the placement of the Praṇava (Praṇava-nyāsa), and after that, the placement of Haṃsa (Haṃsa-nyāsa).
The fifth, consisting of five syllables, is described by the virtuous as Nyāsa. || 36 ||
Among these, one should perform one or several rites, such as worship and so forth, according to the path previously described, by which the state of Śiva is brought about. (37)
One who is not Śiva should not practice Śiva; one who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva;
one who is not Śiva should not meditate upon Śiva; and one who is not Śiva shall not attain Śiva. (38)
Having assumed the Śiva-form, one should then mutter the six-syllabled mantra; having assumed the Śiva-form, one should mutter the six-syllabled mantra along with its limbs.
The Goddess has the syllable *oṃ* as her face and the syllable *vāya* as her two arms.
With the body of a deer, she possesses the two-word mantra "Namaḥ. (39)
The five-syllabled supreme vidyā, together with the star (Tārā), is the form of the Liṅga;
she, in the form of mantra, is to be meditated upon by those possessing authority within Tārā.
Now, listen as I shall speak the mantra for those who are not authorized therein:
the goddess has the face of a hawk and possesses two arms, one of which holds a bow. (41)

The two-word phrase consisting of *visarga* and the middle of the body [the letter *ha*] and the syllable *namaḥ* is the five-syllabled supreme vidyā, which is the *vitārā*, having the form of the *liṅga*.
This very [goddess] should be meditated upon by those twice-born who are devoid of authority over Tāra. || 42 ||
The gross and subtle five-syllabled [mantras] consist of the five parts: *a*, *u*, *mā*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. When combined, they became the *praṇava*, whose nature is the subtle five syllables. (43)
Likewise, "namah śivāya" is the gross five-syllabled mantra; although there is a difference in their magnitude regarding what they signify, no distinction exists between these two. (44)
The subtle root [mantra] is considered its essence, while the elaborate [mantra] is regarded as its detailed exposition;
one who is authorized for the *tāra* (the syllable Om) should recite the mantra joined with that *tāra*.
But one who lacks the qualification for recitation shall go to a downward state by chanting the Tāra mantra. || 45 ||
Although this five-syllabled mantra possesses a power equal to that of Tārā,
it has been [revealed] by the command of the God of Gods, who desires to bestow grace upon the world.
However, for all of them, the command of Śambhu was most weighty and had to be recited as a mantra. || 46 ||

Having performed the ritual for the fire-offering and having recited the Śrī Rudra and other mantras, he should then enter the fire-sanctuary and perform the oblation in the Śiva-fire, which has been consecrated by the Śaiva sacraments.

When the cooking of the *sthālīpāka* has begun, one should prepare the Śaiva [fire] through the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) either in front of or even within the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), and there perform the ritual actions.
The sacrificer should perform the Śaiva rite according to the Vaitānika rules;
likewise, the daily aupāsana rite and the śrauta rites are intended to be performed in that very same place.
One should perform the domestic rites, such as the Vaiśvadeva, according to the Gṛhyaśiva [tradition]. (49)
(124) Regarding the measurement of the sacrificial fuel and so forth: O Lord of Speech, listen as I describe the types of fuel suitable for the oblation.
The sacrificial fuel (samidh) is produced from the palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, śamī, or udumbara trees.
Others know them to be Apāmārga, Dūrvā, and Kuśa grasses. || 50 ||
The fuel sticks should be prepared with their bark intact, straight, smooth, and uniform;
they are recommended to be ten fingers long or twelve fingers long.
They should be fresh or dried, cut evenly, rounded like the thumb and finger,
not fallen, without forked branches, and free from the defects of insects.
The sacrificial fuel (samit), the purifier (pavitra), and the Veda— these three should be one span (prādeśa) in length;
the fuel-sticks (idhma) should be made double that length, and the enclosing sticks (paridhi) are traditionally prescribed to be triple that length.
In the Smārta tradition, the fuel-stick (idhma) is one span long, and the enclosing-stick (paridhi) is traditionally held to be twice that length.
I shall now describe the limbs of the fire and those parts into which one must certainly not offer oblations:
if an offering is made at the ear of the fire, disease results; if at the nose, there is loss of the mind. (54)
The destruction of the eyes is said to result [from offering] on the eyebrows; it would cause poverty if offered on the hair;
there would be sin if offered on the head; therefore, one should offer the oblation on the tongues.
Where there is wood, that is the ear; where there is smoke, that is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; and where there are ashes, that is the head.
Wherever the fire blazes, there alone is the tongue said to be located.
Having thus performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), this salutation (abhivādana) should be performed;
one should complete the first eighth part of the day with these duties.
Regarding the duties to be performed during the second division of the day:
in the second division, one should study the Nigamas and the Āgamas,
teach the Śāstras, and fetch sacrificial fuel and other requirements.
Flowers, bilva leaves, and substances headed by śrīgandha. || 58 ||
One should perform the duties pertaining to the third and fourth parts of the day,
and exert effort toward the accomplishment of one's aims during the third part.
And likewise, during the fourth part [of the day], one should perform the midday bath. || 59 ||
Then, having performed the ash-bath and applied the three marks (tripuṇḍra) according to the rules,
and immediately thereafter, having worn Rudrākṣa beads on the appropriate parts of the body.
One should worship the two twilights with the Sāvitrī, which is the root mantra;
and the five sacrifices must be performed by the householder who desires his own welfare.
Then, the midday worship— whether elaborate, extensive, or brief—
should be performed according to one's ability, with a mind deeply absorbed in devotion.

The worship of the chosen *liṅga* of Maheśvara, which destroys all that is undesirable, should be performed at six times [of the day], or otherwise, three times a day at the junctions of dawn, noon, and dusk. (63)
At the rising of the dawn, at the rising of the sun, likewise at the *saṃgava* period,
at midday, and likewise in the evening and at midnight, O Bṛhaspati.
The flawless Śiva-liṅga should be worshipped at the six times of the day.
Worship performed at the proper time is effective, whereas worship not performed at the proper time is indeed contrary;
whether the worship is small or great, it should be performed according to one's capacity. (65)
Whether he be wise or foolish, beloved or even hateful, whoever arrives at the conclusion of the worship is indeed Śambhu; of this there is no doubt. (66)

One should indeed worship with true devotion a devotee of Maheśvara who has come to one's home; and having propitiated him as a moving image of the deity and having partaken of his grace, [one attains the goal]. 67.
Remaining comfortably and free from anxiety while digesting that food,
one should further recite hymns and ancient Purāṇas dedicated to Maheśa.
Then, in the evening, one should make an effort for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those to be supported.
Having performed the evening duties— whether the Varuṇa bath or the Āgneya bath—
and having worshipped during the evening twilight (sandhyā) and completed the fire-ritual (vahnikārya);
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should then carry out the night worship.
Having honored the guest and enjoyed his favor,
one should recite hymns to Śambhu while digesting that food. (70)
Meditating on Śambhu, one should sleep comfortably upon a bed that is pleasing to lie upon; remembering the pure Śambhu and meditating,
one should sleep free from anxiety, and thereby attain the bliss of sleep.
The dharma to be practiced by the Śāmbhavas has thus been explained to you;
a mortal who conducts himself in this manner is liberated from all sins.
He who, out of atheism or folly, does not practice the Dharma, incurs reproach here in this world and is born into low wombs. (73)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Rule for Daily Rituals," in the section on Action (*kriyāpāda*) within the teaching of Śiva, in the dialogue between Ananta Rudra and Bṛhaspati, in the latter portion of the *Śrīcandrajñānāgama*. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who are devoted to the welfare of all beings!"
For those seekers of liberation belonging to the Śāmbhava tradition, who serve the lotus feet of Śambhu.
O Lord, how can the duties appropriate for the castes and stages of life be considered essential,
when the vow of Śambhu alone is declared to be the supreme means for liberation?
This being so, what fruit is there for devotees of the God of gods in performing various religious duties that actually create obstacles to knowledge? (3)
Anantarudra said:
O Lord of Speech, I shall declare this to you; listen with an attentive mind.
This is the supreme secret, regarding which even the wise are in doubt.
The combination of knowledge and action:
O Sage, knowledge alone is declared by the Supreme Lord to be the giver of liberation;
yet it is taught that when joined with action, it is capable of bestowing liberation. (5)
The blind man, not seeing, was burned; the lame man, seeing, burned [the forest]. Like the blind and the lame, knowledge and action are mutually dependent.
(130) Some people consider even Vedic action to be a cause of bondage;
yet that very same [action], when devoid of knowledge, leads to bondage, while when conjoined with knowledge, it grants liberation. (7)
Furthermore, for one whose mind is rendered helpless through devotion to the meditation on Īśvara, there is in the ultimate sense no bondage by means of action. (8)
Action must certainly not be abandoned even by one who is devoted to the practice of meditation on the Lord,
provided that practitioner remains mindful of the phenomenal world and seeks the welfare of others.
Action regulated by the system of social classes and stages of life must not be abandoned.
That which is not offered to the Lord, that which is performed out of ignorance, and that which is accompanied by a desire for fruit—this is considered to be the cause of bondage. (10)
That which is offered to Maheśa, that which is endowed with knowledge,
and that which is free from the desire for fruit— that is considered to be the cause of liberation.
O bull among sages, the non-commencement of actions does not lead to liberation;
that renunciation of action which is performed merely through intellectual understanding will certainly result in fault.
Established in meditation, he abandons karma like a flower held in the hand of one who is asleep.
O you who are praised by the gods, as long as the mind has not attained Śambhu, the Supreme Self,
so long is it not fitting to completely renounce action. (13)
Therefore, those whose intellects are skilled in the Dharma should respectfully practice the duties appropriate to their respective caste and stage of life; otherwise, one certainly falls. 14.
Having abandoned the conduct of caste and stage of life, yet possessing the power of perfected knowledge,
you will surely fall— of this there is no doubt— like a tree whose supporting branch has been severed.
Therefore, the conduct prescribed for the castes and stages of life, as enjoined by the Vedas and Agamas, must necessarily be constantly practiced by those intent on devotion. 16.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Necessity of the Duties of the Social Classes and Stages of Life," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama.
The first chapter of the Caryāpāda.
Bṛhaspati said:
O abode of infinite knowledge, O abode of radiant compassion!
O Bhagavān Anantarudra, O Teacher of the World, I bow down to you. || 1 ||
The greatness of the Śāmbhava vow has been heard as it appears at the conclusion of the Āgamas;
indeed, the duties of those who observe the Śāmbhava vow are detailed in their entirety within the Kriyāpāda.
It has been received by me from the mouth of the illustrious one with an attentive mind. || 2 ||
Now, please describe the entire procedure for the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) that must be performed for those twice-born who are devoted to this vow and bear its outward signs.
Anantarudra said:
O Lord of Speech, O Sage, listen with a one-pointed mind; I shall describe to you the supreme concluding rite for those devoted to the Śāmbhava vow.
By that very [means] refined, the observer of vows would go to liberation, which is non-origination;
by that very [means] refined, even one devoid of dharma would be liberated at that very moment.
The Description of the Śivamedha:
For those who are steadfast in the Śāmbhava vow and who worship the chosen Liṅga alone,
the great rite of the Śivamedha is to be performed at the end of the body's life.
For those who have entered into the supreme Śiva,
there is a sacrifice consisting of worship known as the Śivamedha; it should be performed by those seeking liberation.
This distinguished Pitṛmedha is called the Śivamedha.
In the Śivamedha sacrifice, one who lacks faith incurs a fall;
in devotion to Śiva, in the worship of Śiva, in the Śivamedha sacrifice, and in the vow of Śiva—
he who dwells without faith shall reside eternally in hell for an inexhaustible time.
Prohibition of Cremation for One Wearing a Śiva-liṅga:
A Brahmin who has died while wearing a Śiva-liṅga should not be cremated;
if one should cremate him, he will always incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
For ordinary men whose souls are devoid of initiation,
the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) accompanied by cremation must indeed be performed at the time of their passing.

The procedure for meditative absorption (samādhi) for those who bear the Śiva-liṅga is enjoined solely for the sake of the purification of those seekers of liberation belonging to the Śāmbhava tradition;
this supreme procedure for meditative absorption is heard of in the Pitṛmedha [section of the Veda]. || 11 ||
For those men who worship the Supreme Lord and are subject to no return [to worldly existence],
the rite for the final end should be performed in conjunction with the rite of meditative absorption (samādhi). (12)

Whether he be a householder, an ascetic, or one bearing a sectarian mark, when he casts off his body, one should not leave that body; rather, at that time, one should preserve it within meditative absorption (samādhi).
This samādhi is the dharma of liberation, which refutes the dharma of the hungry ghosts;
because it is refined by samādhi, no loss of the dharma is to be feared from it. (14)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Praise of the Śiva-Sacrifice," in the Caryāpāda of the Śiva-Śāsana, within the dialogue between Ananta-Rudra and Bṛhaspati, in the latter portion of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 1 ||
The second chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Lord Ananta Rudra, you who are exalted by infinite majesty!
Learn from me what must be done by a man who desires to rise upward. || 1 ||
Anantarudra said: Regarding the instruction on the duties of a person desiring to depart [from the body]: by a man wishing to ascend, his own mind should be fixed upon the Lord.
One should bathe with either ashes or water before performing acts such as giving charity.
Seated upon a seat of kusha grass on the ground, wearing clean washed garments,
one should diligently apply the smearing with sacred ash and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
And rudrākṣas should be worn, O best of sages, according to what has been prescribed.
O Lord of Speech, whoever dies upon this earth wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads attains the state of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.

Having recognized by means of the signs that the imminent departure of the vital breath from one's own self has occurred immediately thereafter, [one should perform] the superimposition of fire upon oneself.
With the verse "yā te agne," the householder should mentally deposit the fires within himself.
One should touch the limbs with ashes while reciting the mantras beginning with "Agni," for the purpose of pacifying this fire that has been superimposed upon oneself.
Indeed, the fire-oblation (homa) in the waters should be performed according to the rules by those purified through the six paths.
The gift of cows, land, gold, and so forth to the devotees of Maheśvara:
"Gold, a cow, land, and the most purifying Śiva-liṅga—these should be given to the devotees of Maheśvara by one desiring union with Śiva. (7)
For you, who have set out for the supreme transcendence in order to achieve the successful departure of the vital breaths, I bestow this cow known as "Transcendence."
For the satisfaction of Mahādeva, who is served by Hiraṇyagarbha,
I have given you gold— the seed of gold that yields great fruit.
For the sake of attaining union with Śiva, which is free from rebirth,
I bestow upon you this most purifying Śivaliṅga. (10)
For the satisfaction of Viśvanātha, whose body is the hundredfold earth,
I bestow upon you this supreme and enduring earth.
Having thus performed acts of charity according to one's ability, one should apply oneself to the principles of reality.
Properly recollecting the mantras beginning with "The life-force of longevity" (āyuṣaḥ prāṇam),
one should then diligently perform the conjunction of all the limbs and the liṅga. || 12 ||
That Liṅga which is known through the instruction of the Guru shines forth— present in all limbs, everywhere, at all times, and facing in all directions.
This one supreme mark alone is well-established within this body;
it shines forth in every direction through the nature of name, form, and action.
The *iṣṭaliṅga* resides in the external limb, the *prāṇaliṅga* likewise within;
and the *bhāvaliṅga* is well-established in this very limb of the self.
The Great Liṅga is in the organ of the heart; the Prasādaka Liṅga is in the organ of the ears;
the Caraliṅga is in the organ of the skin; and the Śivaliṅga is in the organ of sight. || 16 ||
On the limb of the tongue is the *guruliṅga*, and likewise on the limb of the nose;
the *ācāraliṅga* is indeed perpetually well-established. (17)

Just as the subtle body (liṅga) is established in the limbs of the organs of cognition in successive order, so too is the subtle body established in the limbs of the organs of action in successive order. || 18 ||
Inconceivable, indescribable, beyond the reach of speech and mind, possessing all powers, omniscient, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 19 ||
Cultivating that state with a mind purified by contemplation,
he should seek permission from Śambhu’s attendants and perform the rite of atonement.
The rules for expiation concern those [faults] arising from the non-performance of the duties of the castes and stages of life,
as well as those resulting from the violation of vows based on the deficiency of any of the eight coverings.
And those [faults] which arise from the neglect of the fivefold conduct, as well as those born from the neglect of devotion; || 21 ||
"Indeed, for the sake of turning back those defects born of mind and speech, I perform the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta) in the presence of Maheśa. (22)

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "The worship of the Guru and the Living Liṅga," and having worshipped with devotion the Guru, the Carācāra-Īśvara, and the others, and having gratified them with wealth, garments, and other offerings, one should drink the water from their feet (pādatīrtha).
He into whose mouth, at the time of death, the water from the station of Maheśvara is poured,
indeed becomes a purified soul and attains union with Śiva. (24)

Reciting the divine name of Śiva while meditating upon the Great Liṅga, one whose mind is absorbed in Śiva should personally undertake the vow of fasting unto death (prāyopaveśa) while contemplating that Great Liṅga.
Immediately thereafter, the sons and others should cause him to hear the mantras into his right ear—the six-syllable mantra as well as the auspicious Upaniṣads. (26)
Then, at the time of the soul's departure, one should ignite camphor while reciting the mantra for the path beginning with light: "The subtle one is the path. (27)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Practice of the Time of Transmigration," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the venerable Candrajñānāgama. || 2 ||
The third chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Anantarudra, O Blessed One, resplendent with all-encompassing knowledge!
Next, tell me about the function of the agent after the departure [of the soul]. (1)
Anantarudra said:
Regarding the sequence of the agent and the action of departure, I shall first explain the sequence of the agent; listen to that, O you who are honored by the gods.
The son, the grandson, the great-grandson, and likewise the son of a daughter. || 2 ||
His son, or his adopted son, or likewise his lineage;
the one who takes the wealth, the husband, the wife, and even the son of a co-wife. (3)
