Daughter, brother, his son, father, mother, daughter-in-law, as well as granddaughter, daughter’s daughter, the wife of a grandson, and her daughter; || 4 ||
The wife of one to whom [one's father] gave [in marriage], a sister, a sister’s son, a maternal uncle who is a *sodaka*, as well as one who is a *sagotra* or even a disciple of the mother; || 5 ||
The officiating priest, the servant, the teacher, the fellow student, as well as the son-in-law, the friend, and the king are recorded in this sequence. (6)
Regarding the exposition on the rite of the soul's departure:
having observed that the vital breath has departed, the performer, having bathed and put on fresh garments,
and having applied the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and Rudrākṣa beads, does so for the sake of accomplishing his eligibility for ritual action.
One should perform salutations to the Gaṇas and then give wealth as an offering.
Whatever is given on the anniversary of death is superior to giving on all other festival days;
therefore, a son should give wealth according to his ability. (8)
Regarding the occurrence of faults such as leaving food remnants while standing,
one should then perform an expiation;
a seeker of welfare should give a substance that serves as a substitute for the *prājāpatya* penance.
Whether death occurs in a palace or on a couch, one should perform an expiation;
one should give a cow or gold, or else perform the Prājāpatya penance.
(142) For one who has attained accomplishment, it is the time for the rite of consecration;
indeed, once accomplishment is attained, the son of [the lineage] should perform the consecration during the day.
If it remains for twenty-five ghaṭīs before [the next period], it becomes stale. || 11 ||
Whether by day or by night, if that form should remain unrefined,
one should perform its consecration from the very beginning so that it does not become stale.
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated it with the Pāvamānī verses,
and having then bathed it with water, one should duly bury it.

Having performed the refinement for meditative absorption (samādhi-saṃskāra) for the one whose life-force has departed from the body, he should bathe and adorn the corpse with Rudrākṣa beads and sacred ash while reciting the Śrīrudra and other mantras.
Having placed the consecrated liṅga in his hand and worshipped it immediately thereafter,
he should deposit it in a casket and then choose the bearers.
Having placed [the image] in a casket, [one should worship] the eye of the Śiva-grove,
as well as Mahokṣa, Vṛṣabha, Nandīśa, and Nandikeśvara;
with these names joined together, one should [worship] that fourfold body.
Then, having seated him in a celestial chariot, he should lead him to the abode of Śiva.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sequence of the Performer of the Act of Transference," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantaruḍra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the venerable Candrajñānāgama. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O You whose lotus feet are served by the foremost hosts of the Pramathas!
O Anantarudra, O Soul of the Universe, O Blue-throated One, salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
O Maheśāna, please instruct me on all the subsequent duties that must be performed after entering the garden of Śiva. || 2 ||
Anantarudra said:
"The entry of the deceased into a grove sacred to Śiva,
or near a temple of Śiva, or again, into a grove sacred to Śiva— "
Either at the root of a bilva tree or near a sacred bathing place (śivatīrtha) of Śiva.
Having performed the meditative absorption (samādhi) over that body there according to the prescribed rule, and having placed it [there],
one should fill the pit with ashes and also with earth.
Having put on [fresh] clothing, one should then perform a bath with one's clothes on (sacelasnāna). || 4 ||
The necessity of shaving the hair:
"Various sins, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or the theft of gold, reside depending upon the hair; therefore, I shave my hair. (5)
Various sins, equal to Mount Meru and Mandara,
reside depending upon the hair; therefore, I shave my hair.
Having made this formal resolve with the mantra, he should have his hair and beard shaved.
O learned one, he whose crest is knowledge consisting of wisdom—like the crest of a flame—is called "one who possesses a crest"; others are merely wearers of hair.
The rites to be performed after the tonsure: having bathed immediately after the tonsure, and endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
he should obtain the permission of his father for the sake of attaining a divine form.
Then, one should install in meditative absorption a supreme liṅga adorned with nine or five bulls, marked with the names of the ancestors.
One should give the ten gifts and worship the Liṅga thoroughly.
Satiating with milk and other liquids is for the purpose of pacifying the distress produced by the agitation of the earth;
thus, satiation with milk and other substances should be performed daily until the end of the ten-day period.
One should also offer the signs of sacrifice and so forth, and likewise satisfy the ancestors;
one should always present three handfuls of water to the father. (11)
Having entered the house together with his kinsmen, accompanied by a lamp,
he should perform the worship known as "covering the naked" (nagnapracchādana). || 12 ||
The prohibition against moving the *liṅga* installed during a consecration ceremony:
one should not move the *liṅga* installed during a consecration for ten days.
If it has been moved by insects or other causes, one should place it back in its original position.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and touched [the body], one should mutter those vyāhṛtis.
One should worship the linga installed in samādhi for ten days;
by the ritual of ten-day worship, a divine form is produced.
The description of the procedure for propitiation:
thereafter, the propitiation of the father, who possesses a divine form, must be performed according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; by this, the state of Rudrahood becomes certain.
(147) Through the very conjunction with reality, the state of Maheśvara shall arise once again. || 15 ||
On the first day, the third, the fifth, the seventh,
as well as on the ninth and eleventh days, one should perform the ninefold worship (navārādhana).
Up to the seventh generation of relatives and the performer of the rite, having shaved their hair and bathed on the tenth day, they should perform the libation with milk.
One should indeed give the ten gifts according to one's ability, being fully composed.
Having removed the *liṅga* together with the bull-emblem, and having placed that *liṅga* along with the bull upon a cloth,
he should bring it to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) while reciting the mantra: "O Earth, receive this."
There he should emit [the seed], while recollecting the divine form of the Liṅga.
Having thus performed the dismissal and bathed with water containing sesame seeds and *āmalaka* fruits,
one should perform the oblation known as Gāṇapatya and likewise that named Ānanda.
One should perform [this] together with the hosts of ancestors for the attainment of supreme bliss. || 11 ||
On the eleventh day, having bathed and invited learned Brahmins,
and having performed the Rudra-homa sacrifice, one should then carry out the rite of releasing the bull (vṛṣotsarga).
One should release a white bull, or one that is red or even blue,
for the sake of attaining the presence of Śiva through the complete satisfaction of Nandikeśa.
The sequence of the sixteen modes of worship consists of the primary monthly rites and the other sixteen forms of worship,
as well as the worship of the Rudra-gaṇas and that known as the release of the bull (vṛṣotsarga). || 22 ||
One should perform the worship of the fifty Rudras, which is unsurpassed and based upon the six locations characterized by the six signs beginning with right conduct (ācāra). || 23 ||
The first [anniversary rite] should take place on the eleventh day; the ūnamāsika (deficient monthly) rite when a month is deficient;
the traipakṣika (three-fortnightly) rite on the third fortnight; and likewise the ūnaṣāṇmāsika (deficient six-monthly) rite.
It is proclaimed that [the rite] should be performed in the sixth month, slightly less than [six months];
and every month on the anniversary of death, as well as at the end of the year—thus making sixteen [rites]. (25)
Indeed, until the age of sixteen, the state of being a living being does not cease for him;
therefore, worship should be performed for one who has reached sixteen according to the rules for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Without first performing the conjunction with the *tattva*, the sixteenfold rite must not be performed;
this applies to one who desires to perform the conjunction with the *tattva* for the father on the twelfth day.
For indeed, even the sixteen modes of service must necessarily be performed.
That which is performed for the sake of achieving union with reality (tattvasaṃyoga) by designating a single individual according to the rules of the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is proclaimed as the Ekoddiṣṭa.
There is no invocation of the Viśvedevas, nor the recitation of the *nābhiśravaṇa*; there is no circumambulation or formal dismissal, nor indeed any proceeding to the boundary (*sīmānta*). || 29 ||
On the eleventh day, one should worship the Māheśas through the propitiation of Rudra, honoring them in their form as Rudra.
For this is indeed called the propitiation of Rudra, according to the circumstances. || 30 ||
To obtain the fruit of the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), one should honor a single Brahmin;
this is declared to be the worship known as vṛṣotsarga. || 31 ||
One should perform the worship of the fifty Rudras, beginning with Khaḍgeśa, by relying upon the six locations characterized by the six signs, such as conduct and the rest.
Four, six, ten, as well as eleven, twelve, sixteen, and two—these are the deities residing in the six locations beginning with Ācāraliṅga. || 33 ||
Residing in the six signs located within the six cakras beginning with the Ādhāra,
they are situated upon the petals of their respective cakras, numbering four and so forth.
Worshipped in the six locations and abiding in the form of phonemes, these fifty Rudras are indeed to be adored for the satisfaction of the six lingas. (35)
On the twelfth day, however, the conjunction with the principle (tattvasaṃyojana) of the father must be performed with effort for the sake of the cessation of the fourth person.
Indeed, by the very application of the principles (tattva) and so forth, the fourth [state] is indeed brought to cessation. || 36 ||
Regarding one who has become united with the limbs of the *liṅga*, there is a prohibition against the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*):
"When one who is united with the limbs of the *liṅga* dies, the offering of rice balls is not prescribed for that father,
because he has attained the state of Śiva through union with the limbs of the Śiva-liṅga."
That [offering] should indeed be joined as a single lump; it brings about the cessation of the state of being a preta. || 37 ||
The sequence for the propitiation of the *kalā*-tattvas:
having invoked the *kalās* associated with the *tattvas* into the vessel from the various ancestors beginning with Maheśvara, one should then worship the father.
To achieve the unification of the three groups, the son should join the principles (tattvas) and so forth. || 38 ||

By performing the ritual of union with the Tattvas according to the prescribed rule, the perfect attainment of the state of Maheśvara and other such states will undoubtedly accrue to the father and the others. 39.
On the twelfth day, the performer, having invited learned brahmins and obtained the permission of the assembly, should perform the formal declaration (saṃkalpa) as follows. (40)
Intending to perform the ritual application of the principles (tattva-yojana) for his father and his father’s ancestors,
[he addressed] the two Viśvadevas known as Nandikeśa and Mahākāla.
[He is the master] of his father, grandfather, and so forth, who are the very forms of Maheśa and the other [deities],
as well as of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) and the thirty-eight kalās.
One should form the resolve: "I shall perform the propitiation. || 42 ||

Then, having invoked the Viśvedevas, the ancestors and others, as well as the principles (tattvas) and the constituent parts (kalās), and having worshipped them thoroughly, he desired to perform the union of the principles.
One should perform the ten gifts, beginning with the gift of a cow, for the complete satisfaction of the father.
After this, having performed the conjunction of the principles (tattvas) and the digits (kalās),
one should duly perform the Unmāsika and other rites at their appropriate times.
(153) Thus, O Lord of Speech, the ritual for the post-mortem state of those who follow the Śiva-āśrama has been explained to you, in accordance with the Vedas and Āgamas. 45.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rituals for the Deceased," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantaruḍra and Bṛhaspati, in the latter portion of the venerable Candrajñānāgama. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O ocean of infinite virtues, O mine of infinite compassion!
O Lord Anantarudra, I bow down; please show me your grace.
Speak now of the miscellaneous rules regarding the procedures for the funeral rites.
Anantarudra said: O Lord of Speech, I shall explain to you the supreme procedure for miscellaneous rites, which defines the rules for various scattered observances.
By means of which all the doubts of the authors may be completely dispelled. || 2 ||
The group of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa) mentioned previously in the Śaiva and other [traditions], the two Viśvedevas, and those called Rudra and Ananta in the earlier Śaiva [texts],
as well as Skanda, Caṇḍa, and Gaṇeśa, are proclaimed to be the Pitṛs. || 3 ||
Nandī and Mahākāla are the Viśvedevas to the north of that; the Pitṛs, Maheśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva are likewise considered [to be there]. || 4 ||
The ancestors, residing in the world of the Pitṛs, have Vasu and others as their forms;
those residing in my own world shall have Maheśvara and others as their forms. || 5 ||

(p. 155) In Śaiva funeral rites (śrāddha), the following are to be avoided: the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), sesame seeds, the rice-balls (piṇḍa), the scattering of food (vikira), and fire-rites (agnikarma).
And a wise man should avoid using an *arghya* vessel in Śaiva funeral rites (*śrāddha*).
Substances required for ritual use are prohibited in certain scriptural traditions, even if they are mentioned elsewhere;
therefore, let it be understood that what is being prohibited is their absolute necessity.
Sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, incense, a lamp with its wick ready,
flowers, bilva leaves, sacrificial fees, and garments.
Betel, a pellet of ashes, and ritual substances are prescribed for the act of worship.
The sequence for the union with reality:
when the male and female practitioners possess identical *liṅgas*, the practices such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are performed together.
If another perfection is attained prior to *samādhi*, then after that, the practices are performed again.
If the younger brother has performed the funeral rites for their father, and the elder brother arrives later,
he should perform the *tattvasaṃyojana* again, excluding the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
If the eldest brother has already performed the rites for the father, then upon his arrival,
the younger brother should again perform the *pārvaṇa* worship at the end of the ten-day period.
Even the youngest [brother], provided he has established the sacred fires, must indeed perform the application of the principles (tattvayojana).

If, within the ten-day period, another impurity due to death (śāvāśauca) should befall the performer, his purification shall be by means of the remainder of the first period; the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is to be performed as prescribed.
A diligent son should perform the *tattvasaṃyojana* rite for his father and others;
thereafter, when a year has passed, or on the twelfth day, the wise one should do so. (13)
When one performs the *tattvasaṃyojana* again at the end of the year,
it should be performed after the *ūnābdika* and on the day preceding the *ābdika*.
One should perform it on any of the six days beginning from the twelfth day,
or at the end of three fortnights, or at the end of a month, or at the end of a year, or when an auspicious occasion arises.
If, on the very eleventh day, the new moon (darśa) should occur,
one should first perform that [new moon rite] and then carry out the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
Likewise, one should perform [the rites] for the father, the great preceptor, on the thirteenth day.
The arrangement of the *tattvasaṃyojana* and the *ṣoḍaśārādhana*:
if the *ṣoḍaśārādhana* is performed without the *tattvasaṃyojana*, then once a year has passed, one should perform the *ṣoḍaśa* again. (17)
From the *tattvasaṃyojana* onwards, one should unweariedly perform all sixteen rites of propitiation according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
After the conjunction of the principles (tattvasaṃyojana), when one should perform [the rite] again, the wise man should perform it every year in whatever manner he previously performed it. || 19 ||
Having performed the conjunction of the principles (tattvasaṃyojana), one should then proceed as in the Pārvaṇa rite;
this is the eternal rule for the annual worship and other ceremonies.
After the formal unification with reality (tattva-saṃyojana), the rite for a single deceased person (ekoddiṣṭa) is prescribed;
in that case, it should be joined with the divine (daiva), for without the divine portion, it would be in vain.

There is a transgression in failing to perform the conjunction with reality. It is certain that one who performs auspicious deeds without performing the rite of conjunction with reality incurs sin; he will not attain the highest good—this is the settled conclusion.
But when there is another primary agent, one should perform an auspicious rite. || 22 ||
Beginning from the twelfth day and continuing until the end of the year for the sake of satisfaction,
one should offer daily a water-pot filled with water and containing a sacred object of devotion.

For the sake of his father’s attainment of the state of Śiva, one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should perform the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) after the conjunction of the principles (tattvasaṃyojana), following the waning of the moon.
His propitiation is of two kinds and also threefold;
it has been stated that propitiation is twofold, namely *ekoddiṣṭa* and *pārvaṇa*.
Furthermore, it is again threefold: as obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and for a specific desire (*kāmya*). (25)
The annual rite, the new-moon rite, that which is known as the Mahālaya, and the daily rite performed under fixed conditions—these are called the obligatory (nitya) rites. || 26 ||
The conjunction with reality (tattvasaṃyojana) is likewise prescribed for the transit of the sun and for eclipses;
that which is designated as "prosperity" (vṛddhi) is declared to be the occasional rite (naimittika) performed for a single ancestor.

That which is performed on the anniversaries of Manu and the beginnings of the Yugas, as well as generally during the attainable astrological conjunctions (yogas), is designated as "optional" (kāmya).
p.
159) The etymological explanation of the term *śrāddha*:
it is the propitiation of one's parents by men possessing minds of complete faith.
Because it is performed with faith (śraddhā), it is designated as "śrāddha."
If one does not bestow what is requested upon a person who has fulfilled their purpose, that miserly and contemptible-minded individual does not obtain the fruit of that action. (30)
The rules for those who partake in the *śrāddha* are as follows:
when the items have been prepared, one may request what is needed;
otherwise, by eating food that does not satisfy [the ancestors], he would become a slayer of his forefathers. (31)
The recipient should not desire a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the performer should give the sacrificial fee;
both of them would thus have their purpose fulfilled, otherwise they would become vessels of fault.
But if, during the performance of the rite, one says, "I am not capable of providing the sacrificial fee," and the performer likewise does not give it, both of them shall fall into a miserable state.
(160) There is a distinction regarding place, time, and so forth;
in the case of a failure [of memory], it occurs due to place and time, such as when traveling to a foreign land and the like.
And during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should [worship] with gold or silver.
The duty of propitiation is to be performed annually, excluding that which is monthly. || 34 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Miscellaneous Rites," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the illustrious Candrajñānāgama. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Anantarudra, O omniscient one, O master of all the Āgamas!
O Compassionate One, please tell me out of your grace regarding the purification from ritual impurity.
Anantarudra said:
"Impurity is of two kinds, and furthermore, it is fourfold; I shall describe the purification from impurity, so listen attentively, O Sage."
Impurity is said to be of two kinds: that arising from birth and that arising from death.
That is of four kinds: deficient, excessive, complete, and incomplete. (2)

In terms of time, it should be known as either less than or more than three nights; however, that which is incomplete lasts for three nights, while the complete period, O you who are honored by the world of the gods, should be understood as ten days.
Regarding the regulation of days for impurity (āśauca):
in the case of a miscarriage, the mother's impurity lasts three nights, while it does not apply to her kinsmen.
In the case of a full-term birth, the mother's impurity lasts for a number of days equal to the months [of pregnancy], whereas that of the father lasts for three days. (4)
For Brahmins, the period shall be ten days; for kings, twelve days;
for Vaiśyas, it shall be fifteen days; and for Śūdras, one month is prescribed. (5)
Once ten days have passed, however, no impurity arising from birth exists;
for regarding the purification of kinsmen,
when a death or a birth has occurred, the purification of kinsmen comes about through mere bathing alone.
And for siblings and for husband and wife, purification occurs after ten days.
In the case of the death of one who has not been initiated, a period of three days is prescribed for the parents;
however, in the event of the death of one who has been initiated, it is proclaimed that the period lasts ten days.

O Sage, impurity lasts for ten days up to the seventh generation; however, from the fourth to the fourteenth generation, it lasts for three nights; and for the twenty-first generation, there is only the requirement of bathing.
O you who are praised by the gods, it should be known that upon the death of a maternal uncle or similar relative, the impurity lasts for three nights;
however, upon the death of other kinsmen, a period of one day and two nights (pakṣiṇī) is prescribed.
For three nights it shall last; for up to three months, a "pakṣiṇī" [day]; for up to six months, a day and night; for up to a year, a day and night; thereafter, having bathed, one becomes pure. (10)
When several periods of impurity coincide, the cessation of those impurities occurs through a single performance; likewise, purification shall be achieved by that same single performance.
Even if one period is shorter, it ceases along with the first [longer] one.
But impurity belonging to another is superseded by the impurity of the father. || 11 ||
Upon following a corpse, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing, sprinkling himself with ashes,
performing six rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), and beholding Śiva.
There is no occurrence of impurity for ascetics, forest-dwellers, and lifelong students among the social orders;
neither that born of birth nor that born of death exists as impurity here.
The rule for immediate purification is prescribed in the case of a sacrifice, a marriage, a gift, a battle, a national calamity,
and even in times of dire distress. (14)
For all those appointed to perform rites for the gods, for the king, or for the Saṅgha, immediate purification is ordained. || 15 ||
p.
164) The non-application of impurity during the twilight prayers and other such times,
and the purification at the time of one's own ritual duties, is enjoined in all the scriptures.
Therefore, one should not abandon even the twilight worship during a period of ritual impurity. || 16 ||
This complete purification, as enjoined by all the scriptures, has been briefly stated.
O you who are praised by the assembly of sages, what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition on Purity from Impurity," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the venerable Candrajñānāgama. || 6 ||
The seventh chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Ananta Rudra, you who are the support of boundless majesty, salutations be unto you!
Please explain the procedure for expiation, which removes all faults. || 1 ||
Anantarudra said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for expiation, which is the determination of the rules for atonement.
Mortals who die by hanging undoubtedly go to hell.
For them, neither impurity nor the offering of water, nor even meditative concentration, is prescribed. || 2 ||
The expiation for those who carry out the corpses of those who died by hanging:
they touch, follow behind, carry, and even bury the corpse of one who died by hanging, as well as one killed by a cow or a Brahmin.
O Lord of Speech, those men are purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
(p. 166) Regarding the characteristics of the *taptakṛcchra* penance:
one should drink each of the following—hot milk, ghee, and water—on successive days.
And fasting for one night is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*.
For those who dwell in the hermitage of Śiva, there is no such thing as a dry fast;
one should instead practice eating only at night as a substitute for fasting.
A twice-born man should perform penance for association [with outcasts], but he should never associate with those who have fallen;
for by associating for as long as a year, he becomes pure through penance.
Beyond that, it is declared to be equal to that [offense]; he does not deserve expiation for it.
A twice-born man shall perform a three-night *kṛcchra* penance for contact lasting five days;
a *prājāpatya* for ten days, and a *sāntapana* for twelve days.
In half a month it shall be ten nights; in the case of a full month's contact, a *parāka* penance;
for two months, a *cāndrāyaṇa*; and for six months, two *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇa) penances. (8)
If the association lasts for a year, one should diligently perform the Kṛcchra penance;
or, according to the measure of the number of days, one should observe the practice of eating only at night.
168) The expiation for being bitten by a jackal or similar animals:
A twice-born man who has been bitten by a jackal or the like should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred times.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, a twice-born who has been bitten by a dog but once;
Having circumambulated the bull and bathed immediately thereafter, one becomes purified.
The expiation for one killed by a Caṇḍāla or others:
"If one has been killed or died by a Caṇḍāla, or by cows, or by Brahmins,
or even if one has died by poison, one should bury that person without the recitation of mantras."
The carriers shall be purified by the Prājāpatya penance, according to the word of the Brahmins.
Indeed, after a year has passed, an expiation must be performed for one who has died;
having offered the *īśānabali* sacrifice, one should bury the body according to the ritual prescribed for the *pālāśa* tree.
The funeral rites for the deceased must be performed by the sons and others according to the prescribed rules.
The expiation for one who harms living beings such as the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*) and others is as follows:
by killing a ruddy goose, a cock, or even parrots, pigeons, crocodiles, snakes, or *tiṭṭibha* birds, one is purified by eating only at night. (13)
Having killed a man with bones, one should give gold to a Brahmin;
having killed one who possesses no bones, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having killed a thousand [such beings], one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra.
Having killed a mongoose, a rat, an iguana, a vulture, a tortoise, a porcupine, a crow, an owl, or a crane, one is purified after three nights. (15)
Regarding the expiation for conversing with a Caṇḍāla and similar acts: when conversation has been held with a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapāka, one should then,
being self-restrained, perform breath-control once and recite the Sāvitrī mantra.
Upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should bathe; having seen one, one should look at the sun.
But having slept together with Caṇḍālas, one becomes pure after three nights.
Regarding the rules for the purification of vessels and other items:
copper and bell-metal are purified by ash alone; garments by washing with water; and earthenware by discarding them, O Lord of the Great Ones. (18)
When food has been touched by dogs, crows, or vultures, the best of the twice-born should remove a small portion of the contaminated part and discard it along with ashes and water.
Having touched it with a torch of *darbha* grass, it should then be taken up. || 19 ||
Food contaminated by hair, insects, and the like is purified by ashes;
oil is purified by heating, as are clarified butter and milk, by means of a flame. (20)
Wooden vessels are purified by washing, even at that very moment;
a woman is purified by her menses, and a river is purified by its current. (21)
For when wells have been defiled, they attain purity by drawing out water measured by a hundred *kumbhas* and pouring in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). || 22 ||
The ground becomes pure through burning, digging, washing, smearing, rain, and the treading of cows, as well as by the passage of time. (23)
A house defiled by a corpse becomes pure when sprinkled everywhere with water,
smeared with cow-dung, and perfumed with incense smoke.
The sense organs are pure and impure;
those apertures which are above the navel are pure in every respect, while those situated below are impure, as are the excretions that have fallen from the body. (25)
The purification of the impurities residing in the body:
fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, snot, and nails.
Phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. || 26 ||
For the purpose of purifying the discharge of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken as required;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities. (27)
O Bṛhaspati, the purification of the first six impurities is achieved with water and clay; for the latter ones, purification by water alone is desired.
The purification of clothing and other items:
clothing touched by a caṇḍāla is purified by washing;
however, earthenware is purified by discarding it, and grain becomes pure by winnowing. (29)
Food that has been touched by flies, mosquitoes, and the like, or seen by those who are uninitiated, or even touched by hair or insects, becomes pure through the application of ashes.

Soma and the like are never considered "leftovers" (ucchiṣṭa). In the case of Soma, the Madhuparka, an offering presented at the proper occasion, and likewise that which is granted as a favor by one's guru, there is never any state of being "leftover. (31)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Expiation," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the Uttarabhāga of the venerable *Candrajñānāgama*, in the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati. 7.
The eighth chapter.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Anantarudra, O Blessed One, you who are consecrated for the upliftment of the world!
Tell me the expiation for great sins and minor sins.
Anantarudra said:
Regarding the expiations for major and minor sins,
one who has committed a major sin, having approached the presence of a Guru, [should proceed as follows].
Having provided the material for the staff, one shall then attain supreme purification.
Regarding the expiation for approaching those who should not be approached:
for approaching one who is forbidden, the Cāndrāyaṇa vow is declared for the sake of purification.
This applies to a twice-born man who, having fallen under the sway of ignorance, enjoys the company of a Caṇḍālī woman. (3)
Having shaved his hair, including the top-knot, and having subsisted on alms for three years,
he attains purification without doubt by giving a pair of cattle.
One who has approached his father’s wife, his brother’s wife, his teacher’s wife, or his daughter-in-law,
shall perform three Prājāpatya penances and offer two cows as a sacrificial fee.
Having approached an unwilling Brahmin woman, one should perform the Kṛcchra-Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
if she was willing, it shall be half of that. For approaching her once, the Taptakṛcchra is prescribed. (6)
For sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Kṛcchra penance is prescribed; if a pregnancy results, a Sāntapana is ordained.
In the case of a pregnancy from a queen (Kṣatriya woman), it shall be a Parāka; for a pregnancy from a Vaiśya woman, it is declared that three days [of fasting] are required.
But in the case of the womb of a Śūdra woman, there should be an Aindava penance; in this way, one shall be purified, without a doubt.
Having approached a pregnant woman, one who has fallen from her caste, or likewise a woman in her menses, he becomes purified by performing an Atikṛcchra penance; of this there is no doubt.
One should perform the Prājāpatya penance for approaching animals, prostitutes, and the like. || 8 ||
A woman who has been enjoyed once by a sinful man against her will is purified by the menstrual flow associated with Prajāpati; of this there is no doubt.
175) Expiation for striking a sandal and other offenses:
"But upon striking a sandal, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow."
But for eating food from a prison, one should perform the Kṛcchra Sāntapana penance. || 10 ||
Regarding the expiation for eating forbidden food:
having consumed food touched by feces, urine, or semen, or even the food of a Caṇḍāla, or beef, a twice-born man shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (11)
Having eaten the food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), or likewise the leavings of another,
one becomes pure by performing the Kṛcchra penance and then the Brahmakūrca rite.
The expiation for eating at an *ekoddiṣṭa* and similar rites:
"He who eats at an *ekoddiṣṭa* or even at a *tattvasaṃyojana*,
becomes pure by reciting the six-syllabled mantra a thousand times."
Having eaten during the annual worship, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra a hundred times.
176) The expiation for consuming garlic and so forth:
"Milk, garlic, and the fruit of the white eggplant..."
And gṛñjana, and onion, and likewise the exudation of trees. || 14 ||
A Brahmin who has consumed the property of the gods or the food of a Śilīdhra becomes purified by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and eating only at night for three days.
Purity after shaving and similar acts:
A man becomes pure by bathing after shaving, after vomiting, after exposure to the smoke from a funeral pyre, after sexual intercourse, after a bad dream, or upon contact with a wicked person. (16)
The recitation of the Sāvitrī and other mantras possesses the power to destroy even great sins:
ten thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī, two hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas),
twelve ritual baths in a river, or a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrtha) twenty-four miles away.
These four together are equal to a Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance.
One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī, which has a thousand as its maximum, a hundred as its middle, and ten as its minimum; this destroys even the greatest of sins.
By reciting the Vāmadevya hymn three times, one becomes pure on that very day;
by reciting the Pauruṣa Sūkta, one is released from all sin. (19)
By reciting the Rudraikādaśaka, one becomes purified on that very day;
by reciting the venerable Pañcākṣarī, one is purified at that very moment.
By reciting the Atharvaśiras and likewise the Nīlarudra even once,
one is liberated from all sins on that very day.
And by merely reciting the Trisuparṇa, one is liberated from all sins.
Regarding the power of faith to bring about union with Śiva:
"He who performs what is prescribed in the teaching of Śiva solely through faith attains union with Śiva by the grace of Śrīkaṇṭha. (22)
"O Lord of Speech, you have correctly explained the necessity of concealing this scripture— the teaching of Śiva—
which is a secret that must be guarded with great effort among all scriptures. (23)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rules for Expiation," in the Caryāpāda of the Śivaśāsana, within the dialogue between Anantarudra and Bṛhaspati in the Uttarabhāga of the glorious Candrajñānāgama. || 8 ||
The Nyāsa of the Root Five-Syllabled Mantra:
For this venerable Great Root Five-Syllabled Mantra, "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," Vāmadeva is the Seer (on the head),
Paṅkti is the Metre (in the mouth), the venerable Sadāśiva is the Deity (in the heart), Oṃ is the Seed-syllable, Umā...
*Śakti* (at the secret place), *Śiva* as the *kīlaka* (at the feet); the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of pleasing the venerable Sadāśiva during the recitation (*japa*).
This is the sequence of the placement (*nyāsa*) according to the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), intended for celibate students (*brahmacārin*).
The ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*):
*Oṃ yaṃ oṃ*, salutation to the two thumbs, the abode of the power of omniscience;
*Oṃ vāṃ oṃ*, salutation to the two index fingers, the abode of the power of eternal contentment.
Oṃ śīṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of primordial consciousness-power; to the two middle fingers, namaḥ.
Oṃ maṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of independent power; to the two ring fingers, namaḥ. Oṃ naṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of unimpaired power; to the two little fingers, namaḥ.
Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to the abode of infinite power with both palms and backs of the hands. This is the bodily assignment (*dehanyāsa*). Oṃ Yaṃ Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna on the head.
Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa at the face;
oṃ śiṃ oṃ, obeisance to Aghora at the heart;
oṃ maṃ oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva at the private parts.
Oṃ naṃ oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta on both feet.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, obeisance to Praṇava on all limbs. This is the Aṅganyāsa.
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, obeisance to the heart, the abode of the power of omniscience. Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, svāhā to the head, the abode of the power of eternal contentment.
Oṃ śiṃ oṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock, the abode of the power of beginningless awakening.
Oṃ maṃ oṃ, to the abode of independent power, for the armor: Huṃ! Oṃ naṃ oṃ, to the abode of undiminished power, for the three eyes: Vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, to the abode of infinite power, for the weapon: Phaṭ!
p.
182) The sequence of the placement of stability (for householders); the placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
Oṃ śiṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of primordial awakening for the two middle fingers.
Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of eternal contentment for the two index fingers.
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of omniscience for the two thumbs.
Oṃ naṃ oṃ, salutation to the abode of unimpaired power with the two little fingers.
Oṃ maṃ oṃ, salutation to the abode of independent power with the two ring fingers. Oṃ oṃ oṃ, salutation to the abode of infinite power with the palms and backs of the hands.
The placement of the body (*dehanyāsa*):
*Oṃ śiṃ oṃ*, salutation to Aghora at the heart;
*Oṃ vāṃ oṃ*, salutation to Vāmadeva at the secret place.
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta on the two feet;
oṃ naṃ oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna on the head;
oṃ maṃ oṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa on the face.
Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to the Praṇava on all limbs. This is the *aṅganyāsa*:
Oṃ Śiṃ Oṃ, salutation to the abode of primordial awakening power; to the armor, Huṃ.
Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, to the abode of the power of eternal satisfaction, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, to the abode of the power of omniscience, to the weapon, phaṭ!
Oṃ naṃ oṃ, to the abode of the power that is never lost, to the heart, namaḥ!
Oṃ maṃ oṃ, svāhā to the head, the abode of independent power (svatantra-śakti-dhāman).
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā), the abode of infinite power (ananta-śakti-dhāman).
The sequence of the withdrawal-assignment (for forest-dwellers and renunciants):
the hand-assignment.
*Oṃ naṃ*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*) for the abode of unimpaired power.
Oṃ maṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of independence with the two ring fingers.
Oṃ śiṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of primordial awakening with the two middle fingers.
Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of eternal contentment with the two index fingers.
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of the power of omniscience with both thumbs.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, homage to the abode of infinite power with the palms and backs of the hands. This is the deposition on the body (dehanyāsa).
Oṃ naṃ oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta on the two feet;
oṃ maṃ oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva at the secret place;
oṃ śiṃ oṃ, obeisance to Aghora at the heart.
Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa on the face;
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna on the head;
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, obeisance to Praṇava on all the limbs.
The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*Oṃ naṃ oṃ*, to the weapon (*astra*) whose abode is unimpaired power, *phaṭ*. *Oṃ maṃ oṃ*, to the three eyes whose abode is independent power, *vauṣaṭ*.
Oṃ śiṃ oṃ, to the abode of the power of primordial awakening, for the armor, hūṃ! Oṃ vāṃ oṃ, to the abode of the power of eternal satisfaction, for the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ!
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ, to the abode of the power of omniscience, for the head, svāhā!
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, homage to the heart, the abode of infinite power.
